sections.heading: What does a migraine attack feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS says a migraine attack typically brings a throbbing headache, often on one side of the head, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. The cause is unknown, but a migraine happens when there are changes to nerves and blood vessels in the brain, the NHS says.

An attack can pass through several stages, and not every stage occurs every time. The NHS lists early warning symptoms such as unusual tiredness, yawning, food cravings, mood changes, a stiff neck and needing to pass urine more often. These can start hours, or up to two days, before the headache.

The NHS says about 1 in 3 people with migraine have an aura. It can involve zigzag patterns, flashing lights, pins and needles or difficulty speaking. Aura should not last longer than an hour. The Migraine Trust says recovery after the headache can take hours or days.

sections.heading: What types of migraine are there?
sections.body:
The Migraine Trust says migraine without aura is the most common type. Migraine with aura covers several forms, including brainstem aura, retinal migraine, hemiplegic migraine and silent migraine.

A typical aura involves changes in vision, other sensory symptoms such as tingling, or problems with speaking. NINDS says migraine with brainstem aura needs at least two symptoms during an episode, such as vertigo (a spinning feeling), seeing double, trouble with balance or slurred speech.

The Migraine Trust says some people have aura symptoms but no headache, sometimes called silent migraine. Hemiplegic migraine is a rare, severe type involving temporary weakness or paralysis on one side of the body. In vestibular migraine, vertigo, dizziness or unsteadiness are often the main symptoms. The Trust defines chronic migraine as headache on at least 15 days each month.

sections.heading: How is migraine diagnosed?
sections.body:
NICE says a clinician may ask a person to keep a headache diary to help identify the type of headache. The diary records how often headaches happen, how long and how severe they are, and all medicines taken. NICE advises keeping it for a minimum of eight weeks. For migraine that usually happens around a period, the diary should cover at least the next two periods.

A secondary headache is one where another health problem is behind the headaches. NICE says a person may be referred for tests or to a specialist if this is suspected. NICE lists warning signs such as a head injury in the past three months, headaches that start very suddenly, and speech or balance problems that keep getting worse.

NICE advises against referring people with migraine for brain scans solely for reassurance.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for migraine?
sections.body:
The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help with managing attacks and preventing them. For attacks, the NHS lists painkillers, triptans, gepants and anti-sickness medicine, and advises taking painkillers as soon as the headache starts.

The Migraine Trust says gepants can be an option for people who cannot take triptans or for whom triptans do not work, and that they appear not to cause medication overuse headache. It says gepants, CGRP antibodies and flunarizine are usually prescribed by headache specialists rather than GPs.

For prevention, the NHS lists beta blockers, antidepressants, epilepsy medicines, acupuncture, relaxation techniques, cognitive behavioural therapy and vitamin B2. NHS Scotland guidance also lists candesartan and botulinum toxin for chronic migraine.

The Migraine Trust describes medication overuse headache as a headache caused by taking acute migraine medicines too often. It says over-the-counter painkillers, triptans and opioids can cause it. NICE asks clinicians to be alert to it in people whose headaches developed alongside regular use of pain medicines.

sections.heading: Living with migraine: what helps day to day?
sections.body:
The Migraine Trust says triggers usually combine several factors rather than one cause. It names stress, disrupted sleep and skipped meals among the most common, and says shifts in routine often seem to set off attacks. The NHS names periods, stress, tiredness and certain foods or drinks.

The Trust says too little and too much sleep can each trigger attacks, and that regular bedtimes and wake times may help. Some people have attacks when stress eases, such as at weekends. MedlinePlus, a US health site, says regular sleep, exercise and stress management may help.

Foods such as chocolate and cheese are often blamed, but the Trust says the evidence is thin. MedlinePlus describes a headache diary as a way to find triggers.

sections.heading: When should someone get help for migraine?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for a sudden, extremely painful headache, speech or memory problems, loss of vision or double vision, drowsiness or confusion, a seizure, weakness on one side of the body, or a recent head injury. NHS inform likewise advises calling 999 or going to A&E for one-sided weakness or slurred speech.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if an attack lasts longer than 72 hours, if aura lasts longer than an hour, or if the person is pregnant or has recently given birth.

A non-urgent GP appointment is advised if attacks are severe, getting worse, lasting longer than usual, happening more than once a week, hard to control, or regularly happening around a period.

faqs.q: Can migraine be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help with managing attacks and preventing them. MedlinePlus likewise says there is no cure, and treatment focuses on relieving symptoms and preventing further attacks. The NHS says the treatments available depend on how severe the migraine is and how often attacks happen.

faqs.q: Is migraine just a bad headache?
faqs.a: The NHS says a migraine attack typically brings a throbbing headache, often on one side of the head, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people also have an aura, such as zigzag patterns, flashing lights or pins and needles. Early symptoms can include tiredness, food cravings and mood changes.

faqs.q: Can someone have an aura without a headache?
faqs.a: Yes. The Migraine Trust says some people have aura symptoms but no headache, which is sometimes called silent migraine or migraine aura without headache, and that it is more common in older people. The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if aura lasts longer than an hour.

faqs.q: Is a brain scan needed to diagnose migraine?
faqs.a: NICE advises against referring people diagnosed with migraine for brain scans solely for reassurance. Its quality standard says people with tension-type headache or migraine should not be imaged if they have no signs or symptoms of a secondary headache. A clinician may refer for tests or to a specialist if a secondary cause is suspected.

faqs.q: Can painkillers make headaches worse?
faqs.a: The Migraine Trust describes medication overuse headache as a headache caused by taking acute migraine medicines too often. It says over-the-counter painkillers, triptans and opioids can cause it, while gepants appear not to. The Trust recommends speaking to a GP for anyone taking acute medicines frequently.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.definition: A tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures: bursts of abnormal synchronised electrical activity in the brain.
epilepsy.overview: Seizures take many forms depending on where they start: a focal seizure may cause twitching of one hand, an odd smell or a period of unresponsive staring; a generalised tonic-clonic seizure involves loss of consciousness, stiffening and jerking of the whole body. Most people with epilepsy become seizure-free on medication.
causes: Often unknown or genetic
Scarring from stroke, head injury, infection or birth injury
Brain tumours and malformations
Hippocampal sclerosis
Dementia in older people
signs: Usually normal between seizures
Post-seizure confusion, bitten tongue, incontinence
complications: Injury during seizures
Status epilepticus (a seizure over five minutes: an emergency)
Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
Driving and employment restrictions
Depression
epilepsy.diagnosis: A witness account or video is the most useful evidence. An EEG may show epileptic discharges; MRI looks for a structural cause; blood tests exclude metabolic causes and an ECG excludes a cardiac cause of collapse.
epilepsy.treatment: Anti-seizure medication chosen by seizure type (for example levetiracetam and lamotrigine; valproate is avoided in girls and women who could become pregnant because of the risk to an unborn baby), taken consistently. Surgery, laser ablation or nerve stimulation for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Seizure first aid education for family.
epilepsy.prevention: Take medication regularly, sleep well, limit alcohol, avoid known triggers; helmets and safe driving reduce head injuries that cause acquired epilepsy.
epilepsy.seekCare: Call emergency services for a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, a first seizure, injury, or difficulty breathing afterwards.

sections.heading: What are the main types of seizure and what do they feel like?
sections.body:
Epilepsy seizures are grouped by where they start in the brain and how much of it is involved. Focal seizures start in one part of the brain, and some people stay aware during them while for others awareness is affected. Generalised seizures start in, or very quickly affect, both sides of the brain.

Some people notice a warning before a seizure, called an aura. Epilepsy Action says an aura is a type of focal seizure in its own right. Examples include a rising feeling in the tummy, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

In a tonic-clonic seizure the person loses consciousness and the muscles go stiff, so someone who is standing may fall. This is followed by repeated jerking of the arms or legs. A seizure that begins on one side of the brain can also spread to both sides, which is called a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy diagnosed?
sections.body:
Epilepsy Action advises seeing a GP as soon as possible after a suspected seizure, even if the person did not go to hospital at the time. NICE says people with a suspected first seizure should be referred urgently so that a specialist is involved early in diagnosing epilepsy, and its quality standard aims for them to be seen within 2 weeks. Epilepsy Action says anyone with a suspected seizure should have an ECG, a heart tracing, to rule out a heart problem.

No single test can confirm epilepsy. An EEG may be requested, and if it is done after a first seizure it should be done as soon as possible. A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, because many people with epilepsy do not show abnormal activity between seizures. NHS inform says a diagnosis can still be made from the person's description of their seizures even when tests show nothing. NICE recommends an MRI scan for most people who are diagnosed with epilepsy. An MRI scan cannot decide on its own whether someone has epilepsy and is useful alongside other information.

Epilepsy Action advises keeping a seizure diary and taking it to appointments.

sections.heading: How is epilepsy treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says medicine to prevent seizures, called anti-seizure medicine, is the main treatment for epilepsy. NHS 111 Wales says these medicines help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people. They do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. NHS inform says some anti-seizure medicines can reduce how well some types of contraception work. The NHS says it is very important to discuss treatment with a specialist if there is a chance of becoming pregnant while taking epilepsy medicine.

Other options are considered when medicines do not control the seizures. The NHS describes surgery as an option for rare cases. NICE's evidence review describes vagus nerve stimulation as used for people whose seizures have not responded to anti-seizure medicines and who are not suitable for surgery. The ketogenic diet, which is high in fat and low in carbohydrate and protein, is mainly used in children, usually those who have not responded to medicines. NHS inform says it should only be used under the supervision of an epilepsy specialist with the help of a dietitian.

sections.heading: What should happen if someone has a seizure?
sections.body:
NHS advice for a convulsive seizure is to cushion or gently hold the person's head to protect it from injury. Epilepsy Action adds that anything potentially harmful nearby should be cleared. The NHS also advises not restraining the person and not putting anything in their mouth. Once the jerking stops, the advice is to turn the person onto their side in the recovery position.

The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than is usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. A 999 call is also advised if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing. Status epilepticus, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or seizures back to back with no recovery in between, needs emergency treatment, and NHS inform says to phone 999 straight away if it is suspected.

sections.heading: Living with epilepsy and the outlook
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales suggests keeping a seizure diary, noting when seizures happen and what the person was doing beforehand, to help work out triggers. Epilepsy charities and NHS guidance list lack of sleep, missing anti-seizure medicine, stress and alcohol among possible triggers, and the CDC lists hormonal changes with a period. Flashing lights trigger seizures in a small number of people.

GOV.UK says a person must stop driving straight away after any epileptic seizure and tell the DVLA. When driving can start again depends on the type of seizure and how long the person has been seizure-free. Epilepsy can also affect decisions about contraception and planning a pregnancy.

The NHS says an epileptic seizure usually stops by itself and does not cause any lasting problems. Rarely, a seizure can last a long time, or several can happen without recovery in between, which is called status epilepticus and is a medical emergency that needs a 999 call. There is also a small risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). The NHS describes SUDEP as rare and says epilepsy treatment can reduce the risk. The CDC lists frequent or uncontrolled seizures among the factors linked to a higher risk. Epilepsy Action says there is not enough research to show that anti-suffocation pillows reduce the risk.

faqs.q: Can epilepsy be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says anti-seizure medicines do not cure epilepsy, but they can stop seizures happening. NHS 111 Wales says they help control seizures in about 7 out of 10 people. When medicines do not work well enough, other options such as surgery, nerve stimulation or a special diet may be discussed with an epilepsy specialist.

faqs.q: Does a normal EEG mean it is not epilepsy?
faqs.a: No. A normal EEG does not rule epilepsy out, because many people with epilepsy do not show abnormal activity between seizures. No single test can confirm epilepsy. Doctors weigh the EEG together with the story of what happened, any scan results and other information.

faqs.q: Can I drive after a seizure?
faqs.a: GOV.UK says a person must stop driving straight away after any epileptic seizure and tell the DVLA. When they can start again depends on the type of seizure and how long they have been seizure-free. The exception is for people who have already been given permission to drive with their type of seizures.

faqs.q: What is an aura?
faqs.a: An aura is a warning that some people have before a seizure. Epilepsy Action says it is a type of focal seizure in its own right. Examples include a rising feeling in the tummy, unusual smells or tastes, and tingling in the arms and legs.

faqs.q: When should I call 999 for a seizure?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if it is the person's first seizure, if the seizure lasts longer than usual for them, or if it lasts more than 5 minutes and their usual pattern is not known. It also advises calling if the person does not recover as usual, has another seizure before recovering, is seriously injured or has trouble breathing.

parkinsons-disease.name: Parkinson's disease
parkinsons-disease.definition: A progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain are lost, causing slowness, stiffness and tremor.
parkinsons-disease.overview: The basal ganglia need dopamine to release intended movements smoothly. As nigral neurons die, movements become slow and small, muscles stiff, and a resting tremor appears, typically starting on one side. Non-motor features such as loss of smell, constipation, sleep disturbance and later cognitive change are part of the disease. NINDS describes Parkinson's as a chronic, progressive neurological disorder characterised by resting tremor, muscle rigidity, slowness of movement, impaired balance and a shuffling gait. The root causes remain unknown; age, genetics and exposure to environmental hazards are the recognised risk factors. Under the microscope, unusual protein clumps called Lewy bodies form in brain cells. Sleep disorders, constipation and a reduced sense of smell can develop years or even decades before movement problems, and the classical motor features appear only once most of the dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra have already been lost, which is why the diagnosis is often made late.
causes: Accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein in neurons; the trigger is unknown in most cases
Genetic forms in a minority
Rare toxin exposure
riskFactors: Constipation and a history of anxiety or depression as prodromal features
Rural living, farming and well-water drinking
signs: Resting tremor (pill-rolling)
Bradykinesia: slow, small movements
Rigidity (cogwheeling)
Stooped posture, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing
Reduced facial expression, soft voice, small handwriting
complications: Falls and fractures
Swallowing difficulty and pneumonia
Dementia and hallucinations
Depression
Motor fluctuations from long-term levodopa
Orthostatic hypotension and urinary incontinence
Psychosis as a side effect of levodopa in some patients
parkinsons-disease.diagnosis: Clinical, by a neurologist, on the combination of bradykinesia with tremor or rigidity and a response to levodopa. MRI excludes other causes; a DaT scan can confirm dopamine loss when uncertain. Early diagnosis is difficult because early symptoms are often misread as the effects of normal ageing. A large and sustained response to levodopa strongly supports Parkinson's disease over secondary or atypical parkinsonism.
parkinsons-disease.treatment: Levodopa remains the most effective drug; dopamine agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors extend its effect. Physiotherapy, exercise, speech and occupational therapy maintain function. Deep brain stimulation helps selected patients with fluctuations. Levodopa, taken as a tablet or liquid, is combined with benserazide or carbidopa so that it is not broken down in the bloodstream before it reaches the brain. Long-term use is linked to involuntary jerky movements (dyskinesias), 'on-off' effects and wearing-off before the next dose is due, and in some people to psychiatric effects including psychosis. In milder disease clinicians may start with dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors or amantadine to delay levodopa; COMT inhibitors extend its effect. Deep brain stimulation is introduced when medication no longer controls symptoms.
parkinsons-disease.prevention: No proven prevention; regular exercise and coffee are linked to lower risk and exercise slows decline. Caffeine and physical activity appear protective in observational studies, although reverse causation is possible because early disease itself reduces how much people exercise. Smoking is not recommended: the lower rate seen in smokers in these studies does not mean that smoking prevents Parkinson's disease.
parkinsons-disease.seekCare: See a doctor for a new tremor at rest, slowing of movement or a change in gait; urgent help for falls with injury, inability to swallow, or sudden confusion.

sections.heading: What do the symptoms feel like, and how does Parkinson's progress?
sections.body: Parkinson's disease usually develops gradually, and the symptoms are mild at first. The NHS lists three main movement symptoms: tremor, slowed movement and muscle stiffness. The tremor is shaking that typically starts in a hand or arm and is most noticeable when the limb is at rest. Slowed movement is called bradykinesia, and it can lead to a small-stepped, shuffling walk. Slowed movement can make everyday tasks difficult. Stiffness, also called rigidity, can make movement and facial expression harder and sometimes causes painful cramps. The order in which symptoms develop and how severe they are differs for each person. Symptoms generally worsen over time, and the speed of progression varies widely between people.

sections.heading: What other symptoms can happen?
sections.body: Parkinson's also brings symptoms that are not about movement. The NHS and NHS inform list balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. Balance problems can make a fall more likely, and a fall can lead to injury. A loss of the sense of smell sometimes occurs several years before other symptoms develop. The NHS also lists problems sleeping (insomnia) among the symptoms that are not about movement. NHS 111 Wales lists depression, anxiety and dementia among the cognitive and psychiatric symptoms. A review of advanced Parkinson's disease says that late-stage patients develop motor and non-motor complications that can greatly affect quality of life.

sections.heading: How is Parkinson's disease diagnosed?
sections.body: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on the symptoms, the medical history and a detailed physical examination. If Parkinson's is suspected, the GP refers the person to a specialist, such as a neurologist, for a formal diagnosis. Blood tests and brain scans may be used to rule out other conditions. A DaT scan is a brain scan, done in a nuclear medicine department, that looks at dopamine transporters in the brain. It can help tell Parkinson's apart from conditions such as essential tremor, and NICE recommends DaT scans only in selected cases. For the scan, a tracer is injected into a vein and the person lies still, and the report goes to the referring doctor, who contacts the person to discuss the results.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease, but treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life. Treatment can include medicine, therapies such as physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy, and sometimes surgery. Most people with Parkinson's eventually need a medicine called levodopa. The NHS says levodopa usually improves movement problems. MAO-B inhibitors are another option in early Parkinson's disease and give less improvement in movement symptoms than levodopa. When tablets no longer give enough control, some people are considered for levodopa gel delivered through a tube into the small intestine. Another device-aided option is a continuous infusion of apomorphine under the skin. Deep brain stimulation is a type of surgery that does not cure Parkinson's disease but can ease symptoms for some people. It involves implanting a device, sometimes called a brain pacemaker, with leads placed in the brain by stereotactic surgery. It is considered for people whose symptoms are no longer well controlled by oral medicines.

sections.heading: Living with Parkinson's disease
sections.body: Regular exercise can help relieve muscle stiffness, lift mood and reduce stress. Many people with Parkinson's have problems with speech and swallowing. A speech and language therapist can often help by teaching speaking and swallowing exercises. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. Occupational therapists can also provide equipment and strategies that help people stay independent and safe at home. A physiotherapist can work on muscle stiffness and joint pain through movement and exercise. Parkinson's nurse specialists can help arrange referrals to physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy. As the condition advances, it can become increasingly difficult to carry out everyday activities without help.

sections.heading: What is the outlook?
sections.body: NHS 111 Wales says that Parkinson's disease does not directly cause people to die, but it can leave them more vulnerable to serious infections. NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. One single-centre study of hospital admissions found that respiratory infection was the most common cause, at 23% of admissions. A review of palliative care in advanced Parkinson's disease lists aspiration pneumonia, urinary tract infections, complications from falls and fractures, and sepsis from pressure ulcers as the main risks. A separate Rotterdam Study analysis found reduced life expectancy in people diagnosed with parkinsonism, mainly when diagnosis came before age 70. The outlook varies from person to person.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for Parkinson's disease. Treatments are available to help reduce the main symptoms and maintain quality of life, and they include medicine, physiotherapy and occupational therapy. For some people surgery called deep brain stimulation can ease symptoms, although it does not cure the condition.

faqs.q: Can a test confirm Parkinson's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says that no test can conclusively show that someone has Parkinson's disease. A doctor bases the diagnosis on symptoms, medical history and a detailed examination. Blood tests and brain scans may be used to rule out other conditions, and a DaT scan, which looks at dopamine transporters in the brain, may be used when the diagnosis is unclear.

faqs.q: Does Parkinson's disease shorten life?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says that most people with Parkinson's now have a normal or near-normal life expectancy. NHS 111 Wales says the condition does not directly cause death, but it can leave people more vulnerable to serious infections. A Rotterdam Study analysis found reduced life expectancy in people diagnosed with parkinsonism, mainly when diagnosis came before age 70.

faqs.q: Does Parkinson's disease only affect movement?
faqs.a: No, because people can also have balance problems, a reduced sense of smell, nerve pain, bladder problems, constipation, sweating, swallowing difficulties, and changes in mood or memory. The order in which symptoms develop and how severe they are differs for each person. A reduced sense of smell sometimes appears several years before other symptoms.

faqs.q: Who can help with everyday difficulties?
faqs.a: A physiotherapist can work on muscle stiffness and joint pain through movement and exercise. An occupational therapist can pinpoint everyday tasks that are hard, such as dressing or getting to the shops. A speech and language therapist can often help by teaching speaking and swallowing exercises. Parkinson's nurse specialists can help arrange referrals to these therapies.

keyFacts.value: A GP refers people with suspected Parkinson's to a specialist, such as a neurologist.

keyFacts.label: Main medicine
keyFacts.value: Most people eventually need levodopa.

keyFacts.value: Deep brain stimulation can ease symptoms for some people but does not cure the condition.

alzheimers-disease.name: Alzheimer's disease
alzheimers-disease.definition: The commonest cause of dementia: a progressive loss of memory and thinking ability caused by the build-up of amyloid plaques and tau tangles and the death of neurons, beginning in the hippocampus.
alzheimers-disease.overview: Alzheimer's starts years before symptoms, with abnormal proteins accumulating in the medial temporal lobes. Early disease affects the formation of new memories; over years it spreads to language, spatial skills, judgement and finally basic bodily functions. The risk rises steeply with age.
causes: Accumulation of amyloid-beta and tau proteins with loss of synapses and neurons
Rare inherited forms with early onset
riskFactors: Cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, obesity
Low education, hearing loss, social isolation, depression, inactivity
signs: Poor recall of recent events with preserved distant memory
Word-finding difficulty
Getting lost in familiar places
Impaired judgement and planning
Later: personality change, incontinence, immobility
complications: Falls
Infections, especially pneumonia and urinary infections
Malnutrition and dehydration
Carer strain
alzheimers-disease.diagnosis: History from the person and a relative, cognitive testing, blood tests to exclude thyroid, B12 and other reversible causes, and MRI showing hippocampal shrinkage. Amyloid PET or spinal fluid markers can confirm the diagnosis in specialist settings.
alzheimers-disease.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) and memantine give modest symptomatic benefit; anti-amyloid antibodies give a modest slowing of decline in a small group of people with early disease and can cause brain swelling or bleeding; whether they are available depends on national guidance. Structured routines, cognitive stimulation, treating hearing loss and depression, carer support and advance care planning matter as much.
alzheimers-disease.prevention: Up to 40% of dementia is attributable to modifiable factors: control blood pressure, stay physically, socially and mentally active, treat hearing loss, do not smoke, limit alcohol.
alzheimers-disease.seekCare: Forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, getting lost or struggling with familiar tasks over months should prompt a memory assessment; sudden confusion over hours or days is delirium and needs urgent review.

sections.heading: How does Alzheimer's disease feel and progress?
sections.body: The NHS describes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease as becoming increasingly severe as the condition progresses. The Alzheimer's Society says memory loss is usually the first and main symptom in the early stage. The NHS lists trouble finding the right word and poorer judgement as early symptoms, and changes in mood can occur too. Early symptoms also include becoming less flexible and more hesitant to try new things. In the middle stage, existing memory and thinking problems get worse, and many people find it harder to recognise family or close friends. Confusion about time and place becomes more severe, some people develop delusions or hallucinations, and help with daily tasks increases. In the later stage, the NHS lists difficulty eating and swallowing, weight loss and incontinence, which means passing urine or stools unintentionally. NHS 111 Wales says that in the severe stages people may need full-time care and help with eating, moving and using the toilet.

sections.heading: What other types of dementia are there?
sections.body: Alzheimer's is the most common form of dementia, and other common types include vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says around 19 in 20 people with dementia have one of four main types. When someone has more than one type it is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says mixed dementia affects at least 1 in 10 people diagnosed with dementia. Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65. Younger people are less likely to have memory loss as one of their first symptoms, and they are more likely to have a rarer form such as frontotemporal dementia. Mild cognitive impairment is not a type of dementia, but people with it have an increased risk of developing dementia.

sections.heading: How is Alzheimer's disease assessed?
sections.body: For gradual memory problems, the GP is the usual first point of contact. A GP typically asks about symptoms, may examine the person and sets memory and thinking tasks. If the GP is unsure, the person may be referred to a specialist, such as an old age psychiatrist or a neurologist, who may be based in a memory clinic. Blood tests are mainly used to rule out other underlying causes rather than to make the diagnosis itself. According to NHS England, brain scans such as CT or MRI are not essential for a clinical diagnosis. A CT scan can check for signs of a stroke or a brain tumour, and shrinkage seen on a scan may support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease but cannot point to a specific diagnosis. PET scans are typically used when earlier scans are unclear. There is no single test that confirms dementia, so assessment combines the history, memory and thinking tasks and sometimes scans.

sections.heading: What treatments and support are available?
sections.body: The NHS says there is no cure for Alzheimer's disease, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine can be prescribed for early to mid-stage disease, and memantine is used for moderate or severe disease. Non-drug options include cognitive stimulation therapy, which uses group activities and exercises to build memory and problem-solving skills. The NHS describes cognitive rehabilitation as using the parts of the brain that are working to help the parts that are not. Reminiscence and life story work involves talking about things and events from the person's past. The NHS says coping strategies are tried first for aggression, and if they fail a consultant psychiatrist can prescribe risperidone for persistent aggression or extreme distress, using it for the shortest time possible because of its serious side effects. The Alzheimer's Society says lecanemab and donanemab are approved for use in the UK but not on the NHS. NICE's final draft guidance said their benefits remain too small to justify the additional costs to the NHS, so the NICE website has the current position.

sections.heading: Living with Alzheimer's disease and caring for someone
sections.body: NHS inform suggests keeping in touch with people and joining activities, and notes that dementia-friendly groups, communities, sport and cultural activities exist for people with dementia. It says a daily routine can encourage feelings of security, value and worth. Suggested memory aids around the home include pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside, and technology such as a device that plays a recorded reminder when the front door is opened. Local councils provide information about aids and adaptations for the home, and memory services can offer memory aids and strategies. Depression is common in dementia, and NHS inform says a GP can talk through talking treatments that can help. A care needs assessment can be arranged through social services, and carers can ask the local council for a carer's assessment. NHS inform describes advance care planning as thinking ahead about which treatments a person would want, including whether they would want certain end-of-life treatments.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body: The Alzheimer's Society says the middle stage of dementia is often the longest. In the later stage many people have trouble eating or swallowing, which can lead to choking, chest infections and other problems. Delirium is a sudden change in mental state, where the person seems not themselves, and it is different from the slow worsening of dementia. The Alzheimer's Society says dementia can make a person much more likely to have delirium. Urinary tract infections can cause sudden and severe confusion in someone with memory problems or dementia, and confusion can also be a sign of a stroke or sepsis. NHS services such as South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust advise going to A&E or calling 999 if someone suddenly becomes confused. The Alzheimer's Society advises making an urgent GP appointment or calling NHS 111 for a sudden change in someone with dementia. Once the cause is treated, symptoms usually improve within a few days for many people, though some have memory and thinking problems for longer.

faqs.q: Is Alzheimer's disease the same as dementia?
faqs.a: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, but it is not the only one. The Alzheimer's Society says around 19 in 20 people with dementia have one of four main types. Some people have more than one type, which is called mixed dementia, and the most common mix is Alzheimer's disease with vascular dementia. Young-onset dementia is dementia that begins before the age of 65.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for Alzheimer's disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure, but some medicines can temporarily ease symptoms or, for some people, slow progression. Non-drug approaches such as cognitive stimulation therapy and reminiscence work are also used. A care needs assessment can be arranged through social services, and carers can ask the local council for a carer's assessment.

faqs.q: Will I need a brain scan?
faqs.a: According to NHS England, brain scans such as CT or MRI are not essential for a clinical diagnosis. A CT scan can check for signs of a stroke or a brain tumour, and shrinkage seen on a scan may support a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease. PET scans are typically used when earlier scans are unclear.

faqs.q: Why might someone with dementia suddenly become much more confused?
faqs.a: A sudden change is different from the slow worsening of dementia and may be delirium. Urinary tract infections are one cause of sudden and severe confusion in someone with dementia. NHS services advise going to A&E or calling 999 for sudden confusion, and the Alzheimer's Society advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a sudden change in someone with dementia.

faqs.q: Do memory problems always mean dementia?
faqs.a: Memory problems are not always caused by dementia, so the GP may look for other causes. A GP typically asks about symptoms, may examine the person and sets memory and thinking tasks. Blood tests are mainly used to rule out other underlying causes rather than to make the diagnosis itself. If the GP is unsure, the person may be referred to a specialist, who may be based in a memory clinic.

keyFacts.value: Symptoms become increasingly severe over time, says the NHS.

keyFacts.value: Memory loss is usually the first and main symptom, says the Alzheimer's Society.

keyFacts.label: Most common form of dementia
keyFacts.value: Alzheimer's disease.

keyFacts.label: Medicines used
keyFacts.value: Donepezil, galantamine and rivastigmine for early to mid stages, and memantine for moderate or severe disease.

keyFacts.label: Non-drug support
keyFacts.value: Cognitive stimulation therapy, cognitive rehabilitation and reminiscence work.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the airways causing reversible narrowing, with episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough.
asthma.overview: In asthma the bronchial lining is chronically inflamed and over-reactive. Triggers such as allergens, viruses, exercise or cold air make the smooth muscle constrict and the lining swell and pour out mucus. Between attacks breathing may be normal. It affects about one child in ten and one adult in twelve.
causes: Genetic susceptibility plus environmental exposure: allergens (dust mite, pollen, pets), early viral infections, tobacco smoke, air pollution, occupational chemicals
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or allergy
signs: Widespread wheeze on breathing out
Fast breathing, use of accessory muscles in an attack
A silent chest and exhaustion in a life-threatening attack
complications: Severe attacks needing hospital care
Airway remodelling and fixed narrowing
Side effects of repeated steroid courses
asthma.diagnosis: Variable symptoms plus evidence of variable airflow obstruction: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, peak-flow variability, or raised exhaled nitric oxide and blood eosinophils.
asthma.treatment: Inhaled corticosteroids are the foundation, combined with a long-acting bronchodilator as needed; a reliever inhaler for symptoms; a written action plan; trigger avoidance; biologic injections for severe allergic or eosinophilic asthma. Attacks are treated with high-dose reliever, oral steroids and oxygen.
asthma.prevention: Avoid smoking and smoke exposure, control allergens, have flu vaccination, use the preventer inhaler daily and check inhaler technique.
asthma.seekCare: Emergency care if the reliever is not helping, the person cannot speak in sentences, lips are blue, or peak flow is below a third of best.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms and triggers of asthma?
sections.body:
The NHS lists coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and breathlessness as the main symptoms of asthma. They are often worse at night and early in the morning, or when a trigger is present. Asthma involves swelling, called inflammation, of the breathing tubes that carry air in and out of the lungs.

The NHS says it is not fully understood what causes asthma. Risk factors it lists include a family history of asthma or atopic conditions (conditions linked to allergy), childhood exposure to tobacco smoke, and being born prematurely or at low birth weight.

The NHS lists common triggers such as infections like colds and flu, allergens such as pollen, dust mites and animals, smoke, pollution, weather, mould or damp, and exercise. Some cases are linked to substances in the workplace, which is called occupational asthma.

Asthma + Lung UK says frequent use of a reliever inhaler is a sign that asthma is not well controlled, and advises speaking to a GP, nurse or pharmacist.

sections.heading: How is asthma diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP will typically ask about symptoms and triggers, and may ask about eczema, allergies or a family history of them. There is no single test for asthma. A diagnosis is made from the symptom history and the results of breathing tests.

The NHS lists FeNO, spirometry and peak flow among the main tests. In a FeNO test a person breathes into a machine that measures nitric oxide in the breath, which is a sign of inflammation in the lungs. Spirometry measures airflow and lung volume. Peak flow testing uses a handheld device over a few weeks.

The UK guideline from NICE, BTS and SIGN sets out an order of tests. For children aged 5 to 16 with a history suggestive of asthma, FeNO comes first, followed by spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility. Peak flow measurements over a period of time are used if spirometry is unavailable or delayed.

sections.heading: What are the treatments for asthma?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for asthma, but treatment can help control the symptoms. Inhalers are the main treatment. Reliever inhalers are used when symptoms occur. Preventer inhalers are taken daily to reduce inflammation in the airways.

Asthma + Lung UK explains that a blue reliever inhaler opens the airways but contains no steroid, so it cannot reduce inflammation. The charity says NICE guidelines recommend that no one with asthma should have only a blue reliever inhaler, and that anyone using one also needs a steroid preventer.

Some people use a single combination inhaler called an anti-inflammatory reliever. It contains a steroid and a reliever medicine and is taken only when symptoms appear.

The NHS says tablets may be added if inhalers alone are not controlling symptoms. If asthma is severe and not controlled by inhalers and tablets, injected medicines called biological therapies may be offered. Only an asthma specialist can prescribe them, and they suit only specific types of severe asthma.

sections.heading: Living with asthma: action plans, reviews and outlook
sections.body:
The NHS lists useful steps such as always carrying an inhaler, avoiding known triggers and having vaccinations such as the flu vaccine. A person with asthma will usually have a personal asthma action plan.

Asthma + Lung UK says an action plan helps a person understand their symptoms and what to do if they get worse. It is arranged in traffic-light sections. Green covers everyday care, amber covers worsening symptoms, and red covers the signs of an asthma attack, what to do, when to call 999 and when to contact the GP afterwards.

The NHS says steroid tablets may be used as a short course during an attack, or daily over the long term only in very severe asthma. Long-term or frequent use can cause side effects, including fragile bones (osteoporosis), so people are monitored regularly.

MedlinePlus says there is no cure, but with self-care and medical treatment most people can live normal lives. It adds that symptoms sometimes ease over time, especially in children, and that attacks can be life-threatening and are more common in people with severe asthma.

sections.heading: What happens in an asthma attack, and when should I call 999?
sections.body:
The NHS describes an asthma attack as having severe symptoms and difficulty breathing, which can be life-threatening. NHS 111 Wales lists a reliever inhaler that is not helping, and breathlessness that stops a person speaking, eating or sleeping, as signs of an attack.

NHS 111 Wales advises sitting up, trying to stay calm and taking puffs of the reliever inhaler. It says to call 999 for an ambulance if a person feels worse at any point, or does not feel better after taking the puffs.

NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing, gasping or choking. NHS information also says to contact a GP urgently if a person is more short of breath than usual despite using inhalers as prescribed.

faqs.q: Can asthma be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for asthma, but treatment can help control the symptoms. MedlinePlus says symptoms sometimes ease over time, especially in children, and that with self-care and medical treatment most people can live normal lives. Inhalers are the main treatment.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
faqs.a: Reliever inhalers are used when symptoms occur and quickly relax the airways to make breathing easier. Preventer inhalers are taken daily to reduce inflammation in the airways. Asthma + Lung UK says a blue reliever inhaler contains no steroid, so it cannot reduce inflammation, and that anyone using one also needs a steroid preventer.

faqs.q: What tests are used to diagnose asthma?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no single test for asthma. A diagnosis is made from the symptom history and the results of breathing tests. The tests it lists are FeNO, which measures nitric oxide in the breath, spirometry, which measures airflow and lung volume, and peak flow testing with a handheld device over a few weeks.

faqs.q: What is an asthma action plan?
faqs.a: An asthma action plan helps a person understand their symptoms and what to do if they get worse. Asthma + Lung UK describes green sections for everyday care, amber for worsening symptoms and red for an asthma attack. The red section covers the signs of an attack, what to do, when to call 999 and when to contact the GP afterwards.

faqs.q: When does an asthma attack need a 999 call?
faqs.a: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathing difficulty, such as struggling to speak without pausing, gasping or choking. NHS 111 Wales says to call 999 for an ambulance if a person feels worse at any point, or does not feel better after taking puffs of the reliever inhaler.

keyFacts.value: No cure, but treatment can help control the symptoms (NHS).

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
copd.definition: Progressive, largely irreversible airflow obstruction caused by damage to the airways (chronic bronchitis) and destruction of alveoli (emphysema), almost always from smoking.
copd.overview: Years of inhaled smoke inflame the small airways and dissolve the alveolar walls, so air is trapped and the surface for gas exchange shrinks. Breathlessness on exertion creeps up over decades and is often blamed on age; flare-ups triggered by infections drive hospital admissions. COPD is the third leading cause of death worldwide.
causes: Tobacco smoking (85 to 90% of cases)
Biomass and cooking-fire smoke
Occupational dust and fumes
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (inherited)
riskFactors: Childhood respiratory infections and poor lung growth
signs: Barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing
Wheeze and reduced breath sounds
Cyanosis and ankle oedema in advanced disease
complications: Exacerbations, often needing hospital care
Respiratory failure
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale)
Lung cancer
Osteoporosis, muscle wasting, depression
copd.diagnosis: Spirometry showing an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator, in someone with symptoms and a smoking or exposure history. Chest X-ray and CT exclude other causes and grade emphysema.
copd.treatment: Stopping smoking is the only measure that slows decline. Long-acting bronchodilator inhalers (with inhaled steroids for frequent exacerbators), pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, and oxygen at home for low oxygen levels. Exacerbations are treated with steroids and often antibiotics.
copd.prevention: Never smoking, or stopping at any stage; clean cooking fuels; workplace dust control; vaccination against flu, pneumococcus and COVID-19.
copd.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathlessness, blue lips, chest pain, or new confusion or drowsiness (a sign of carbon dioxide retention). Get same-day advice from a GP or NHS 111 for worsening breathlessness with more or discoloured sputum, or fever.

NHS Scotland: Mental health and wellbeing in COPD

sections.heading: What does COPD feel like, and how does it change over time?
sections.body:
The NHS describes COPD as a lung disease that develops slowly, so symptoms are often not noticed early on. The main symptoms are breathlessness during activity, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheezing. Phlegm is the thick mucus coughed up from the airways. Several other conditions, such as asthma, heart failure and anaemia, can cause similar symptoms.

The NHS says COPD cannot be cured or reversed. For many people, treatment helps keep it under control so that it does not severely limit daily activities. For some people it keeps getting worse despite treatment and can lead to life-threatening problems. The NHS says that the sooner treatment starts, the less chance there is of severe lung damage.

sections.heading: What are emphysema and chronic bronchitis, and what causes COPD?
sections.body:
COPD is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. Emphysema and chronic bronchitis are two of the conditions grouped under it. Chronic bronchitis is inflammation of the airways, which leads to a long-term cough with mucus. Emphysema is damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs, which reduces the elasticity of the lungs. Many people have features of both.

Smoking is the biggest risk factor. The NHS estimates that it is behind around 9 in 10 cases, and the risk rises with how much and for how long a person smokes. The WHO lists long-term exposure to dust or fumes at work, air pollution, and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as other factors. In the United States, CDC data show that some adults with COPD have never smoked. The condition usually emerges after the age of 35.

sections.heading: How is COPD diagnosed, and what do the tests show?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP starts by asking about symptoms and about whether the person smokes or used to smoke. The GP examines the chest, listens to the breathing with a stethoscope, may calculate body mass index and asks about any family history of lung problems. The GP may then do, or arrange, a breathing test called spirometry. NICE guidance says COPD is suspected from symptoms and signs, and that spirometry supports the diagnosis.

A chest X-ray can look for other lung problems that cause similar symptoms, such as chest infections and lung cancer, although these do not always show. Blood tests can detect conditions such as anaemia, and sometimes check for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a rare genetic problem that increases the risk of COPD. A CT scan, which is a detailed scan of the lungs, or a phlegm sample to check for infection is sometimes needed to confirm the diagnosis or judge severity.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for COPD, and what are they for?
sections.body:
The NHS says stopping smoking is the most effective way to prevent COPD getting worse. Damage already done to the lungs and airways cannot be reversed, but giving up smoking can help prevent further damage. Short-acting bronchodilator inhalers, which widen the airways, are usually the first treatment. Long-acting bronchodilator inhalers may be recommended if there are regular symptoms or flare-ups. A GP may add a steroid inhaler if breathlessness or flare-ups continue, and this is normally given in a combination inhaler. NICE favours keeping the number and types of inhalers to a minimum, because that makes it easier to use them correctly. It also says inhalers should only be prescribed after people have been trained to use them.

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised programme of exercise, education and breathing techniques, usually in groups. Oxygen is useful only for people whose blood oxygen is low, and it is not a treatment for breathlessness. Lung volume reduction surgery, which removes badly damaged lung tissue, and lung transplant are options for only a small number of people.

sections.heading: What is a flare-up, and how do people live with COPD?
sections.body:
A flare-up, also called an exacerbation, is a time when symptoms are worse than usual. MedlinePlus describes one as increased symptoms lasting two days or more. Infections are a common cause. Treatment may include quick-relief inhalers, steroids or antibiotics taken by mouth, or oxygen if it is prescribed. Asthma + Lung UK describes an agreed written action plan as central to managing flare-ups. MedlinePlus suggests pursed-lip breathing to save energy, slow the breathing and help a person relax.

Common advice also includes taking medicines as prescribed and avoiding smoke, dust and fumes. The NHS encourages everyone with COPD to have the annual flu jab and the one-off pneumococcal vaccination. NHS Scotland says mental health difficulties are more common in people with COPD than in the general population.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help with COPD?
sections.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP about persistent symptoms such as breathlessness, a chesty cough with phlegm or frequent chest infections, especially for someone over 35 who smokes or used to smoke. That is a GP appointment rather than an emergency.

For someone already diagnosed, MedlinePlus lists breathing that is getting harder, faster or shallower, fever, dark mucus, sleepiness, confusion, chest pain or bluish lips or fingertips as reasons to contact a provider. In the UK, urgent but non-emergency advice comes from NHS 111 or the GP the same day. South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust says to call 999 if someone with COPD is very unwell with severe breathlessness, chest pain or coughing up blood.

faqs.q: Can COPD be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says COPD cannot be cured or reversed, and damage already done to the lungs and airways cannot be undone. For many people, treatment helps keep it under control so that it does not severely limit daily activities. The NHS lists stopping smoking, inhalers and pulmonary rehabilitation among the options.

faqs.q: Is COPD the same as emphysema?
faqs.a: COPD is the name for a group of lung conditions, and emphysema is one of them. Emphysema is damage to the tiny air sacs in the lungs. Chronic bronchitis, which is inflammation of the airways leading to a long-term cough with mucus, is another. Many people have features of both.

faqs.q: Do only smokers get COPD?
faqs.a: No. Smoking is the biggest risk factor, and the NHS estimates it is behind around 9 in 10 cases. Other factors include long-term exposure to dust or fumes at work, air pollution, and a rare inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. CDC data from the United States show that some adults with COPD have never smoked.

faqs.q: What is a COPD flare-up?
faqs.a: A flare-up, or exacerbation, is a time when COPD symptoms are worse than usual. MedlinePlus describes it as increased symptoms lasting two days or more. Infections are a common cause. Asthma + Lung UK describes an agreed written action plan as central to managing flare-ups.

faqs.q: What does pulmonary rehabilitation involve?
faqs.a: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a supervised programme of exercise, education and breathing techniques. It is usually run as group sessions over several weeks, and some people use remote or app-based versions. The NHS lists it among the treatments for COPD, alongside stopping smoking and inhalers.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.definition: Infection of the alveoli, which fill with fluid and inflammatory cells so that part of the lung cannot exchange gas.
pneumonia.overview: Bacteria (most often Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses (influenza, COVID-19, RSV) and occasionally fungi cause pneumonia. It ranges from a mild illness treated at home to a life-threatening one in the elderly, the very young and those with chronic disease, and it remains the leading infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
causes: Bacteria: pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Staphylococcus
Viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV
Aspiration of stomach contents
Hospital-acquired organisms in ventilated or frail patients
riskFactors: Weak immune system, diabetes, heart, kidney or liver disease
signs: Fast breathing, fever, crackles and dull percussion over the affected lobe
Low oxygen saturation
Confusion in the elderly
complications: Pleural effusion and empyema
Sepsis
Respiratory failure
Lung abscess
pneumonia.diagnosis: Clinical findings plus a chest X-ray showing consolidation. Blood tests (white cells, CRP, kidney function), oxygen saturation, sputum and blood cultures, and a severity score (CURB-65) guide where and how to treat.
pneumonia.treatment: Antibiotics chosen by likely organism and severity (amoxicillin for mild community-acquired pneumonia; combinations in hospital), antivirals for influenza, oxygen, fluids, and support of breathing in severe cases. Rest and hydration at home for mild cases.
pneumonia.prevention: Pneumococcal, influenza and COVID-19 vaccination, stopping smoking, good hand hygiene, and managing chronic diseases.
pneumonia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, confusion, blue lips, chest pain, coughing blood, or fever with fast breathing in a child or older adult.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pneumonia?
sections.body:
The NHS says pneumonia symptoms can come on suddenly or build up over a few days. A cough, breathlessness and a fever are typical, and chest pain and confusion can also occur, with confusion being common in older people. Some people cough up yellow or green phlegm. Where the lining around the lung is also inflamed (pleurisy), the chest pain can be sharp and get worse when breathing.

The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough that lasts about three weeks or more, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness. It advises calling 999 for severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, sudden confusion or coughing up more than streaks of blood, and says not to drive yourself to A&E. Pneumonia is more common, and can be more serious, in young children.

sections.heading: What causes pneumonia, and what are the complications?
sections.body:
Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs. Bacteria, viruses or fungi can cause it. The pneumococcus bacterium can cause pneumonia, and the vaccine against it is described below.

Aspiration, which means food or liquid going down into the lungs by mistake, can also cause pneumonia.

Pneumonia can affect people of any age. Pneumonia can be more serious in young children, in people over 65 and in people with other serious health problems, who are more likely to need hospital care.

Complications of pneumonia can include pleurisy, fluid around the lungs, a lung abscess, sepsis and respiratory failure.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia diagnosed?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets describe a doctor first asking about symptoms and examining the chest. A chest X-ray may be arranged to confirm the diagnosis, and blood tests and tests on a sample of phlegm (sputum) may also be done.

Doctors often use a scoring system to gauge how serious the pneumonia is. NHS inform describes a scoring system called CRB-65 that estimates the risk of complications and whether urgent hospital treatment is needed. Most people recover at home, while people who are very unwell or at higher risk may be admitted.

In hospital the team can give antibiotics through a drip, and sometimes steroids, and may add oxygen to help breathing. The NHS says a follow-up chest X-ray is not routine for everyone. It may be arranged about six weeks later for some people, for example those who smoke or are over 50.

sections.heading: How is pneumonia treated, and how long does recovery take?
sections.body:
The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause. Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, plenty of rest and plenty of fluids. Pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics.

People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital. There the usual treatment is antibiotics, often given into a vein, and sometimes steroids. Oxygen can be added to help with breathing.

Recovery varies from person to person. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline: the high temperature should have gone after about a week, chest pain and mucus should have reduced substantially after about four weeks, and cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks. Most symptoms should have resolved by three months, although tiredness can linger, and most people feel back to normal by about six months.

Recovery can take longer in older people and in people with other health problems. The cough may last for two to three weeks after the antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer as the body recovers. People who have had pneumonia are also more prone to other chest infections for a while.

sections.heading: Can pneumonia be prevented?
sections.body:
The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against serious illnesses such as pneumonia, but it does not protect against illnesses caused by other bacteria or viruses. The pneumococcal vaccine helps protect against serious pneumococcal infections, which can lead to pneumonia, septicaemia and meningitis.

In the UK the pneumococcal vaccine is offered to babies as part of the routine childhood programme. The pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is given to people aged 65 and over and to people at high risk because of long-term health conditions. The NHS also offers flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines to some groups, such as older people and people with certain long-term health conditions.

faqs.q: Do all cases of pneumonia need antibiotics?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says antibiotics are the usual treatment when bacteria are the likely cause, but pneumonia caused by a virus does not need antibiotics.

faqs.q: Can pneumonia be treated at home?
faqs.a: Mild cases can often be treated at home with antibiotics, rest and plenty of fluids. People who are very unwell, or at higher risk, may be treated in hospital, where antibiotics are often given into a vein and oxygen can be added.

faqs.q: Why does the cough last so long after pneumonia?
faqs.a: The NHS and hospital leaflets say a cough can carry on for two to three weeks after antibiotics are finished, and tiredness can last longer. NHS guidance sets out a rough timeline in which cough and breathlessness should have eased substantially after about six weeks.

faqs.q: When is pneumonia an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, sudden confusion or coughing up more than streaks of blood, and not to drive yourself to A&E. For a cough that lasts about three weeks or more, yellow or green phlegm or breathlessness it advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine against pneumonia?
faqs.a: There are vaccines against some causes. The pneumococcal vaccine is offered to babies and to people aged 65 and over or at higher risk. Flu, RSV and COVID-19 vaccines are also advised for specific groups, but vaccines do not cover every cause of pneumonia.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the lining of the airways or alveoli, divided into non-small-cell (about 85%) and small-cell types.
lung-cancer.overview: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death because it is usually found late: symptoms appear only when a tumour blocks an airway, invades the chest wall or spreads. Smoking causes about eight in ten cases. Low-dose CT screening of eligible heavy smokers can find lung cancer at an earlier stage, when treatment is more likely to be curative. Early lung cancer often causes no symptoms at all. The NHS lists a persistent cough, breathlessness, coughing up blood and chest or shoulder pain as the main features; less common ones are swelling of the face or neck, difficulty swallowing from pressure on the oesophagus, a hoarse voice that does not go away from pressure on the laryngeal nerves, and clubbing of the fingers. Bone pain and facial or eyelid changes tend to appear late. The cause is not always known: lifestyle, genetic changes and environmental factors all contribute, with smoking the largest single risk. A targeted screening programme using low-dose CT is being rolled out in England for eligible older adults, aimed at finding cancer before symptoms appear.
causes: Tobacco smoke
Radon gas
Asbestos, diesel exhaust and other occupational carcinogens
Air pollution
Family history
Arsenic and other industrial chemicals
signs: Finger clubbing
Hoarse voice
Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
Signs of a pleural effusion or collapsed lobe
Weight loss
Swelling of the face or neck
Wheeze, or difficulty swallowing from a tumour pressing on the oesophagus
Bone pain and facial or eyelid changes in late disease
complications: Spread to lymph nodes, liver, bones, brain and adrenals
Airway obstruction and pneumonia
Superior vena cava obstruction
Paraneoplastic syndromes
Compression of the oesophagus (swallowing difficulty) and of the laryngeal nerves (hoarseness)
lung-cancer.diagnosis: Chest X-ray then CT of the chest and abdomen; tissue by bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy; PET-CT for staging; molecular tests on the tumour to guide targeted therapy. A GP asks about symptoms and general health and may check lung function with a spirometer. A chest X-ray is usually the first test but cannot give a definitive answer on its own, so a specialist arranges a CT scan and a bronchoscopy, in which a thin tube with a camera is passed through the mouth or nose into the airways to take a biopsy that shows the cancer type; a PET-CT scan shows where active cancer cells are. Pathology is reviewed by a specialist lung cancer pathologist before treatment because small-cell cancer can be mistaken for other types. Staging uses the TNM system (tumour size, lymph node spread, distant metastasis) and tells the team whether a complete cure is possible; small-cell cancer is described as limited stage when confined to one half of the chest within a single radiotherapy field, otherwise extensive stage.
lung-cancer.treatment: Depends on type and stage: surgery or radical radiotherapy for early non-small-cell cancer; chemotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted drugs (for EGFR, ALK and other mutations) for advanced disease; chemotherapy and radiotherapy for small-cell cancer; palliative care for symptoms throughout. The choice depends on the type, size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread, specific genetic changes and the person's general health. Surgery is the main curative treatment for non-small-cell cancer and may be combined with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy. Small-cell cancer responds well to chemotherapy and is generally not treated surgically. Radiotherapy can cause breathlessness and a hoarse cough during treatment, which usually ease in the weeks afterwards.
lung-cancer.prevention: Not smoking is the single most effective measure; radon testing of homes; workplace protection; CT screening for eligible heavy smokers.
lung-cancer.seekCare: NHS advice is to see a GP for a cough lasting longer than three weeks, unexplained breathlessness, weight loss or a new hoarse voice, especially with a history of smoking; coughing up blood warrants an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111; and struggling to breathe or pain in the chest or upper back warrants 999 or A&E. Anyone with symptoms is advised not to wait for a screening appointment.

sections.heading: What are the main types of lung cancer?
sections.body:
Lung cancer is mostly divided into two groups, called non-small cell and small cell lung cancer. MedlinePlus says non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 85 percent of lung cancer, and small cell lung cancer accounts for the remaining 15 percent. Non-small cell lung cancer includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma is the most common of these.

Knowing the type matters. The NHS says treatment depends on the size of the cancer and where it is, the type of lung cancer, whether it has spread, whether it has certain genetic changes and the person's general health. It also says surgery is not usually used to treat small cell lung cancer, because the cancer has often already spread to other areas of the body by the time it is diagnosed.

sections.heading: How is lung cancer staged?
sections.body:
Cancer Research UK says the TNM system is the most common way to stage lung cancer, and that TNM stands for Tumour, Node and Metastasis. The number staging system uses TNM to group lung cancer into different stages, which run from 1 to 4.

Small cell lung cancer may also be described as limited or extensive stage. Cancer Research UK says this is a simpler and older system, and that doctors are using it less often as they learn more about small cell lung cancer. Macmillan describes limited stage as cancer cells that can be seen in one lung and in nearby lymph nodes, and extensive stage as cancer that has spread outside the lung, to the chest area or to other parts of the body. The National Cancer Institute defines extensive stage as TNM stage IV with distant metastases.

Roy Castle says that stage 4 lung cancer is not curable, but it is treatable, and many people can live well with advanced cancer.

sections.heading: What happens during tests for lung cancer?
sections.body:
A chest X-ray is usually the first test for lung cancer. It often cannot give a definitive diagnosis on its own. A CT scan is usually the next test.

If a CT scan suggests a tumour in the central part of the lung, a bronchoscopy lets the doctor look inside the airways and remove a small sample of cells. Another option is a CT-guided needle biopsy, in which a thin hollow needle is passed through the chest wall into the lung. Macmillan says a doctor usually numbs the skin first with an injection of local anaesthetic. A chest X-ray afterwards is the standard way to check for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax), which is a known risk of the biopsy.

A PET-CT scan is typically used when a CT scan has shown cancer. A biopsy is usually how doctors confirm lung cancer.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for lung cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says that you may be offered a combination of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and targeted medicines, and that immunotherapy may also be used.

For non-small cell lung cancer, the NHS says surgery is generally the first option when the cancer is in one lung and the person is in good health, and it may be followed by a course of chemotherapy. If the cancer has spread too far for surgery or radiotherapy to be effective, chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy is usually recommended. Cancer Research UK says radiotherapy can be used on its own, instead of surgery, for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer, and that it can also be combined with chemotherapy.

Small cell lung cancer is usually treated with chemotherapy, either on its own or in combination with radiotherapy. Targeted medicines are used when a specific molecular target is found in the tumour, so cancer cells are tested to see whether a targeted drug may suit. NHS 111 Wales says targeted therapies cannot cure lung cancer, but they can slow its spread.

sections.heading: What is living with lung cancer like?
sections.body:
Cancer Research UK says that a cough or breathlessness can be early symptoms after radiotherapy to the chest, and that these settle within a few weeks of finishing treatment. Scarring or inflammation in the treated lung can cause breathlessness or a cough later on, and this might start months after treatment, so Cancer Research UK advises telling a doctor about any changes in breathing or increased mucus.

A lung cancer clinical nurse specialist can give information and emotional support and can refer you on to other services. Your GP is responsible for your care at home, community or district nurses can make regular home visits, and palliative care nurses can also phone or visit you at home to check that symptoms are being managed.

After treatment, Cancer Research UK says you are likely to have an appointment with your doctor within 4 to 6 weeks after the treatment has finished, and that visits then become less frequent over time..

faqs.q: What is the difference between non-small cell and small cell lung cancer?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus says non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 85 percent of lung cancer and small cell lung cancer for the remaining 15 percent. Non-small cell lung cancer includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma. The NHS says small cell lung cancer is usually treated with chemotherapy, either on its own or in combination with radiotherapy, and that surgery is not usually used for it.

faqs.q: Is advanced lung cancer treatable?
faqs.a: Roy Castle says that stage 4 lung cancer is not curable, but it is treatable, and many people can live well with advanced cancer. The NHS says that if non-small cell lung cancer has spread too far for surgery or radiotherapy to be effective, chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy is usually recommended.

faqs.q: Why are tumours tested for genetic changes?
faqs.a: Targeted medicines are used when a specific molecular target is found in the tumour, so cancer cells are tested to see whether a targeted drug may suit. NHS 111 Wales says targeted therapies cannot cure lung cancer, but they can slow its spread.

faqs.q: What happens after lung cancer treatment ends?
faqs.a: Cancer Research UK says that after surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy you are likely to have an appointment with your doctor within 4 to 6 weeks after the treatment has finished and that visits then become less frequent over time. Tests at some visits might include blood tests, X-rays, a CT scan or a PET-CT scan.

faqs.q: What happens in a lung needle biopsy?
faqs.a: A CT-guided needle biopsy passes a thin hollow needle through the chest wall into the lung, with a CT scan guiding where the needle goes. A chest X-ray afterwards is the standard way to check for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax), which is a known risk of the procedure.
