appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.definition: Acute inflammation of the appendix, usually because its opening into the caecum is blocked.
appendicitis.overview: The appendix is a blind pouch hanging off the caecum in the lower right abdomen. When its lumen is obstructed, by a hard pellet of stool, swollen lymphoid tissue or rarely a tumour, bacteria multiply, pressure rises, the wall becomes inflamed and, within a day or two, can perforate. It is the commonest cause of emergency abdominal surgery. The classic story is pain that begins around the navel and, over hours, shifts to the lower right abdomen, becoming sharper and worse with movement, coughing or sneezing; loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, a low fever and abdominal swelling commonly follow. The picture is less typical in young children, older adults and pregnant women, in whom the diagnosis is often delayed. In many cases no specific cause is identified.
causes: Obstruction of the appendix lumen by a faecolith or enlarged lymphoid tissue
Rarely a tumour or parasite
Multifactorial in many cases; often no specific cause is found
signs: Tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant
Rebound tenderness
Pain on the right when the left side is pressed (Rovsing's sign)
Mild fever and fast pulse
Abdominal swelling and reluctance to move
complications: Perforation and peritonitis
Abscess
Sepsis
Bowel obstruction from adhesions
Delayed diagnosis in children, older adults and pregnancy, raising the chance of rupture
appendicitis.diagnosis: Largely clinical: the migrating pain, right lower quadrant tenderness and raised white cells and CRP. Clinicians take a history and examine the abdomen, then use urine tests to exclude a urinary infection or kidney stone, blood tests for inflammation, and a pregnancy test in women to exclude an ectopic pregnancy. Imaging confirms the diagnosis or finds another cause of the pain: ultrasound first in children and in pregnancy, CT in adults when the picture is unclear, and MRI where radiation is to be avoided.
appendicitis.treatment: Prompt removal of the appendix (appendectomy), now usually laparoscopic, with antibiotics before and, if perforated, after surgery. Selected uncomplicated cases can be treated with antibiotics alone, with a risk of recurrence. An abscess may be drained first and the appendix removed later. Prompt surgery lowers the risk of rupture. Appendicectomy is performed laparoscopically through small incisions or, when needed, through an open incision (laparotomy), with antibiotics given before surgery and continued afterwards if the appendix has perforated. A ruptured appendix, an abscess or peritonitis needs specialised care: an abscess may be drained under imaging guidance and the appendix removed at a later date.
appendicitis.prevention: None proven. Because appendicitis cannot be prevented, outcomes depend on early recognition and prompt surgery before the appendix ruptures.
appendicitis.seekCare: Same-day emergency assessment for pain that moves to the lower right abdomen, worsens over hours, and comes with nausea, loss of appetite or fever. Severe pain with a high fever may mean the appendix has ruptured and needs immediate hospital care; untreated appendicitis can progress to peritonitis or an abscess, so people are advised not to wait to see whether the pain passes.

gerd.name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
gerd.definition: Reflux of stomach acid into the oesophagus often enough to cause symptoms or damage the lining.
gerd.overview: The lower oesophageal sphincter normally keeps acid in the stomach. When it relaxes too often or is weakened, especially with a hiatus hernia or obesity, acid burns the unprotected oesophagus. Heartburn after meals and lying down is the classic symptom; chronic reflux can scar the oesophagus or change its lining (Barrett's oesophagus), a precursor of cancer. The anti-reflux barrier is made up of the lower oesophageal sphincter and the crura of the diaphragm that wrap around it; transient relaxations of the sphincter are the commonest mechanism of reflux, with a hiatus hernia, raised abdominal pressure and poor clearance of refluxed acid from the oesophagus adding to it. Heartburn and regurgitation are the typical symptoms, but reflux can also present with chronic cough, asthma, laryngitis or dental erosion in the absence of heartburn, which makes it harder to recognise. Large or late meals, irregular meal timing, smoking, obesity and some medicines all contribute; the evidence linking specific foods is limited and varies between individuals.
causes: Weak or over-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter
Hiatus hernia
Raised abdominal pressure: obesity, pregnancy
Delayed stomach emptying
Transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Poor clearance of refluxed acid from the oesophagus
riskFactors: Alcohol, coffee, fatty and spicy food, large late meals
Some drugs: NSAIDs, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates
signs: Usually none
Dental erosion, hoarseness
complications: Oesophagitis and ulcers
Strictures causing difficulty swallowing
Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma
Chronic cough, asthma worsening, laryngitis
gerd.diagnosis: Typical symptoms responding to acid suppression are usually enough. Endoscopy is done for alarm features (difficulty swallowing, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, onset over 55) or persistent symptoms; pH monitoring quantifies reflux when the diagnosis is unclear. Other causes of similar symptoms, such as eosinophilic oesophagitis, are considered. Upper endoscopy is recommended when alarm features are present or when symptoms do not respond to a proton pump inhibitor; it shows oesophagitis, strictures and Barrett's change and allows biopsy. Oesophageal pH monitoring confirms abnormal acid exposure when the diagnosis remains unclear.
gerd.treatment: Weight loss, smaller earlier meals, raising the bed head, avoiding triggers, stopping smoking. Antacids and alginates for occasional symptoms; proton pump inhibitors for regular symptoms and healing. Anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) for severe cases. Lifestyle changes are a core part of management and can sometimes control symptoms on their own: dietary adjustments, raising the head of the bed, not lying down soon after eating and stopping smoking. Proton pump inhibitors are the standard first-line medicine; concerns about long-term side effects and about symptoms returning when they are stopped have driven research into newer drugs. Symptoms that persist despite a proton pump inhibitor (refractory reflux) prompt further evaluation to exclude other causes before escalating; endoscopic therapies and anti-reflux surgery such as fundoplication help people whose symptoms are clearly reflux-triggered.
gerd.prevention: Healthy weight, not smoking, moderate alcohol and coffee, no large meals within three hours of bed.
gerd.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, collapse, or chest pain that could be cardiac. See a GP promptly for difficulty or pain swallowing, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, or heartburn that persists despite treatment.

sections.heading: What does GORD feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes heartburn as a burning feeling in the middle of the chest, often with a sour taste, caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat. It is often worse after eating, when lying down and when bending over. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

NHS inform lists other possible symptoms, including bloating, belching, vomiting, a hoarse voice and a sore throat. NIDDK, a United States institute, describes GERD (the American spelling) as a more severe and longer-lasting condition in which reflux of stomach contents into the oesophagus, the food pipe, causes repeated symptoms or complications.

The NHS says common triggers include coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate, and fatty or spicy foods. Smoking, being overweight, pregnancy, stress and some painkillers such as ibuprofen are also listed.

sections.heading: Is reflux different in babies and children?
sections.body:
NICE guidance on reflux in children and young people describes regurgitation, when a baby brings milk back up, as common and normal in infancy. The NHS says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight, and that babies usually grow out of it by the age of 1. It suggests a GP visit if a baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

For formula-fed babies who often regurgitate and are very distressed, NICE sets out steps for clinicians. These include reviewing the feeding history, trying smaller, more frequent feeds, and then trying a thickened formula.

A children's hospital leaflet lists coughing, gagging, trouble swallowing and wheezing among the symptoms to raise with a GP or health visitor.

sections.heading: How is GORD diagnosed, and are tests needed?
sections.body:
NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from the symptoms and may start treatment without any tests. NIDDK likewise says doctors usually diagnose it from symptoms and medical history. Testing is generally kept for people whose symptoms do not improve with lifestyle changes and medicines, or where a complication or another condition is suspected.

The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy may be used for severe or persistent cases. A gastroscopy is an examination in which a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat to look at the lining of the food pipe and stomach.

NHS inform advises seeing a GP if symptoms happen several times a week, if over-the-counter medicines are not helping, or if there are signs of something more serious such as persistent vomiting, vomiting blood or unexplained weight loss. The NHS notes that severe chest pain can occur and may be mistaken for a heart attack, and says urgent medical help is needed rather than a routine appointment. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for GORD?
sections.body:
The NHS says pharmacies sell antacids, which neutralise stomach acid, and alginates, which form a coating that protects the oesophagus from acid. These ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods.

If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, a GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor. This is a medicine, such as omeprazole or lansoprazole, that reduces how much acid the stomach makes. The NHS says some people need to take it on a long-term basis. If it does not control symptoms, a medicine known as an H2 receptor antagonist may be recommended.

The NHS says surgery is rarely needed. NHS inform describes it as an option if medication does not control symptoms.

sections.heading: Living with reflux: what self-care helps?
sections.body:
The NHS lists several self-care measures. These include eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding trigger foods, and not eating within three to four hours of bed. It also suggests avoiding tight waistbands, not smoking, cutting back on alcohol and losing weight if needed. Raising the head of the bed may also help, but the NHS says extra pillows are not recommended.

NIDDK says that for people who are overweight or have obesity, a doctor may suggest losing weight. It lists foods and drinks commonly linked to symptoms, including citrus fruits, tomatoes, chocolate, mint, caffeine, alcohol, high-fat foods and spicy foods. It adds that people react differently, so a doctor may suggest cutting out particular foods to see what helps.

sections.heading: What problems can reflux cause?
sections.body:
NHS inform says long-term damage to the oesophagus from leaking stomach acid can lead to ulcers, scarring and changes to the cells of the oesophagus, which can increase the risk of oesophageal cancer. A hospital leaflet says narrowings of the oesophagus, called strictures, are most commonly caused by scarring from acid reflux and usually cause difficulty swallowing that develops gradually.

Barrett's oesophagus is a change in the lining at the lower end of the oesophagus, usually found through endoscopy. Hospital leaflets say long-term acid reflux is thought to be the main driver, and the changed cells are not cancerous but carry a small increased risk of becoming so. NICE guidance says a history of reflux symptoms and obesity are the main risk factors.

NHS inform says a hiatus hernia, where part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm, makes reflux more likely.

faqs.q: Is acid reflux the same as heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS describes heartburn as the burning feeling in the chest from acid travelling up towards the throat. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD. So heartburn is the symptom, and GORD is the longer-lasting condition behind it.

faqs.q: Do antacids cure GORD?
faqs.a: The NHS says antacids and alginates ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods. A pharmacist can advise on them. If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, the NHS advises seeing a GP, who may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces how much acid the stomach makes.

faqs.q: Is a camera test always needed for reflux?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from symptoms and may start treatment without tests. The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy, where a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat, may be used for severe or persistent cases.

faqs.q: Do babies grow out of reflux?
faqs.a: The NHS says babies usually grow out of reflux by the age of 1. It says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight. It suggests a GP visit if the baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeing a GP if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, if heartburn happens most days, or if there are other symptoms such as food getting stuck in the throat, frequent sickness or weight loss for no reason. Severe chest pain needs urgent medical help rather than a routine appointment; in an emergency, call 999.

peptic-ulcer.name: Peptic ulcer
peptic-ulcer.definition: A break in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that extends through the mucosa, caused by acid acting on a weakened defence.
peptic-ulcer.overview: Most peptic ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by NSAID painkillers, both of which strip the mucus barrier that protects the lining from acid. Duodenal ulcers are commoner and classically hurt when hungry; gastric ulcers hurt after eating. Ulcers can bleed or perforate. Only a minority of people infected with H. pylori go on to develop ulcer disease. Symptoms include pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen, feeling full too soon during or too full after a meal, nausea, bloating and belching, though some people have no pain and small ulcers may cause no symptoms at all. Bleeding can be slow and subtle, so the only clue may be tiredness and weakness from anaemia rather than visible blood. As awareness and treatment of H. pylori have grown, bleeding ulcers are increasingly linked to NSAID use, older age and other illnesses.
causes: Helicobacter pylori infection
NSAIDs and aspirin
Rarely: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe physiological stress, Crohn's disease
riskFactors: Steroids and anticoagulants taken with NSAIDs
Other illnesses (comorbidity) in older people, now a leading context for bleeding ulcers
signs: Epigastric tenderness
Signs of anaemia if bleeding chronically
Rigid abdomen if perforated
Pallor and tiredness from slow blood loss
Early fullness, bloating and belching reported in the history
complications: Bleeding: vomiting blood or passing black stools
Perforation and peritonitis
Gastric outlet obstruction
Gastric cancer (with H. pylori)
peptic-ulcer.diagnosis: Testing for H. pylori (breath, stool or blood test); endoscopy to see the ulcer, take biopsies and treat bleeding, especially in those over 55 or with alarm features. Testing for H. pylori is advised for anyone with a current or past ulcer. At endoscopy a rapid urease test on a biopsy, with or without histology, is usually the first test; if it is negative, a urea breath test or serology follows. An upper GI contrast series is an alternative where endoscopy is not performed.
peptic-ulcer.treatment: Eradicate H. pylori with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics for one to two weeks; stop NSAIDs; proton pump inhibitor for four to eight weeks to heal. Bleeding ulcers are treated endoscopically; perforation needs surgery. Eradicating H. pylori heals the ulcer and reduces the chance of rebleeding. For NSAID-related ulcers the NSAID is stopped and acid suppression given; if the NSAID cannot be stopped, a proton pump inhibitor is continued alongside it, and misoprostol or a lining-protecting medicine such as sucralfate may be added. Prescribed aspirin or NSAIDs are not stopped without medical advice, since they may need adjusting rather than withdrawal.
peptic-ulcer.prevention: Avoid NSAIDs when possible or take a protective proton pump inhibitor with them, stop smoking, limit alcohol.
peptic-ulcer.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools, sudden severe abdominal pain, or collapse. MedlinePlus lists sudden sharp abdominal pain, a hard, rigid, tender abdomen, fainting, heavy sweating or confusion, vomiting blood, and maroon or black tarry stools as reasons for urgent care.

gallstones.name: Gallstones
gallstones.definition: Hard deposits, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder when bile becomes supersaturated.
gallstones.overview: Gallstones are present in about one adult in ten and most cause no trouble. Symptoms begin when a stone blocks the gallbladder outlet (biliary colic), inflames the gallbladder (cholecystitis), or escapes into the bile duct where it causes jaundice, infection of the bile (cholangitis) or pancreatitis. Bile is a mixture of cholesterol, bile pigment (bilirubin) and bile salts; stones form when it holds too much cholesterol or bilirubin, or too few bile salts to keep them dissolved. Only a minority of people with silent stones ever develop symptoms. When a stone lodges in the gallbladder outlet or a bile duct the result is biliary colic: a sudden, severe pain in the upper abdomen that lasts for hours and then eases. Nausea, indigestion and bloating on their own are not specific to gallstones. Persistent pain with fever or jaundice means the gallbladder has become inflamed or a stone has moved into the bile duct.
causes: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile with sluggish gallbladder emptying
Pigment stones from red cell breakdown (haemolysis) or infection
Too little bile salt or excess bilirubin in bile
signs: Right upper quadrant tenderness worse on breathing in (Murphy's sign)
Fever in cholecystitis
Jaundice with a duct stone
complications: Acute cholecystitis and empyema
Bile duct obstruction and cholangitis
Acute pancreatitis
Gallstone ileus
Gallbladder cancer (rare)
gallstones.diagnosis: Ultrasound shows stones and a thickened gallbladder wall; liver function tests and lipase detect duct obstruction and pancreatitis; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound finds duct stones. Clinicians combine the history, examination and tests: blood tests show inflammation or infection and whether the bile ducts, gallbladder, pancreas or liver are affected, and ultrasound is the first imaging investigation because it shows stones, gallbladder wall thickening and duct dilatation without radiation.
gallstones.treatment: Silent stones need no treatment. Symptomatic stones: laparoscopic removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy), ideally within days of a cholecystitis attack; duct stones are removed endoscopically (ERCP). Pain relief, fluids and antibiotics for infection. NIDDK describes removal of the gallbladder as the usual treatment for symptomatic stones, and almost all are now done laparoscopically. Non-surgical treatment with medicines to dissolve cholesterol stones is sometimes used when surgery is not possible, but pigment stones do not dissolve and need surgery.
gallstones.prevention: Healthy weight lost gradually, regular meals, a diet high in fibre and low in refined carbohydrate.
gallstones.seekCare: Urgent assessment for abdominal pain lasting more than a few hours, pain with fever or shivering, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. A stone blocking the bile duct causes sudden pain that needs medical attention right away.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.definition: Chronic inflammation of the gut driven by an abnormal immune response: ulcerative colitis affects the colon's lining continuously from the rectum; Crohn's disease can affect any part of the tract, in patches and through the full wall thickness.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.overview: IBD typically begins in the teens and twenties and follows a relapsing course. Ulcerative colitis brings bloody diarrhoea and urgency; Crohn's brings pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, mouth ulcers and complications such as strictures and fistulas. Modern immune-modulating drugs control most cases, but surgery is still needed by many.
causes: Interaction of genes, the gut microbiome and an over-active mucosal immune response
Over 200 susceptibility genes identified
riskFactors: Smoking (for Crohn's; it is protective in ulcerative colitis)
NSAIDs and antibiotics may trigger flares
signs: Weight loss, anaemia
Abdominal tenderness or a mass
Perianal fistulas and skin tags in Crohn's
Mouth ulcers, eye inflammation, joint swelling
complications: Severe colitis and toxic megacolon
Strictures, fistulas and abscesses
Anaemia and malnutrition
Colorectal cancer after long-standing colitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
inflammatory-bowel-disease.diagnosis: Blood tests (anaemia, CRP), faecal calprotectin to distinguish from irritable bowel, stool cultures to exclude infection, colonoscopy with biopsies, and MRI of the small bowel for Crohn's.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.treatment: Aminosalicylates for mild ulcerative colitis; steroids to settle flares; thiopurines, methotrexate and biologic antibodies (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-23) or JAK inhibitors to maintain remission; nutritional therapy in Crohn's; surgery for complications or refractory colitis.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.prevention: No known prevention; not smoking reduces Crohn's flares and complications.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for more than six bloody stools a day with fever or a fast pulse, severe abdominal pain and distension, or inability to keep fluids down.

colorectal-cancer.name: Colorectal (bowel) cancer
colorectal-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the colon or rectum, almost always arising from a benign polyp (adenoma) over years.
colorectal-cancer.overview: Bowel cancer is the third commonest cancer worldwide. Because it grows slowly from polyps, screening by stool testing and colonoscopy can find and remove growths before they turn malignant. Early cancers are cured by surgery; symptoms usually appear late, so screening participation matters. Early cancers may produce no symptoms, which is why screening is offered to people who feel well: it finds cancers at the stage when treatment is most effective and removes precancerous polyps before they turn malignant. Where symptoms occur they depend on where the tumour sits and whether it has spread, and all of them, including bleeding and a change in bowel habit, also occur in benign conditions, so they are not diagnostic on their own. Treatment is planned by stage, from stage 0 (confined to the lining) to stage IV (spread to distant organs), and the cancer can recur after treatment, so follow-up continues for years.
causes: Accumulated genetic mutations in the lining cells, usually sporadic
Inherited syndromes: Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis
riskFactors: Processed and red meat, low fibre, obesity, inactivity
A personal history of adenomas (polyps) or a previous bowel cancer
signs: Change in bowel habit lasting weeks
Blood in or on the stool
Iron-deficiency anaemia
A palpable mass
Weight loss
Narrower stools, diarrhoea or constipation persisting for weeks
complications: Bowel obstruction or perforation
Spread to liver, lungs and peritoneum
Anaemia
colorectal-cancer.diagnosis: Faecal immunochemical test for screening or triage, then colonoscopy with biopsy; CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging; MRI of the rectum; blood CEA marker. Screening uses a faecal immunochemical test (FIT) that detects hidden blood in the stool; a positive test or new symptoms lead to colonoscopy, which allows the whole colon to be inspected, polyps removed and the tumour biopsied. Once cancer is confirmed, staging determines treatment: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis looks for spread to the liver and lungs, MRI of the pelvis defines how far a rectal cancer has grown through the wall and towards nearby structures, and the blood marker CEA gives a baseline for follow-up.
colorectal-cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove the tumour and lymph nodes is the mainstay; chemotherapy after surgery for higher-risk disease; radiotherapy and chemotherapy before surgery for rectal cancer; chemotherapy, targeted and immune drugs for spread; liver metastases are sometimes resectable. The National Cancer Institute's PDQ summary describes surgery as the most common treatment at every stage. For stage 0 a polypectomy or local excision with clear margins may be enough, with colon resection for larger lesions; for stages I and II the standard operation is wide resection of the affected segment with its lymph nodes and rejoining of the bowel (anastomosis). Chemotherapy after surgery is the established approach for stage III disease and is still under evaluation for stage II. Rectal cancer is often treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy before surgery to shrink the tumour. For stage IV and recurrent disease the options include surgery, systemic chemotherapy, targeted and immune therapies and clinical trials; liver metastases may be treated by resection, chemotherapy before or after surgery, local ablation or chemotherapy delivered into the hepatic artery.
colorectal-cancer.prevention: Take part in screening from the age offered, eat fibre and less processed meat, keep active and a healthy weight, do not smoke, limit alcohol; aspirin lowers risk in Lynch syndrome. Diet, body weight and physical activity have some of the strongest links to risk of any cancer type, so these are the modifiable factors with the most to gain.
colorectal-cancer.seekCare: See a doctor within days for blood in the stool, a change in bowel habit lasting three weeks, unexplained weight loss or anaemia; emergency care for severe pain with vomiting and a swollen abdomen.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of bowel cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a change in bowel habit, blood in the poo, bleeding from the bottom, ongoing tummy pain, unexplained weight loss and ongoing tiredness among the possible symptoms of bowel cancer. The NHS says having these symptoms does not definitely mean bowel cancer, but it is important to get checked by a GP. Several UK sources advise seeing a GP when a change in bowel habit lasts three weeks or more.

Blood in the poo can have harmless causes such as haemorrhoids (piles), but it should always be checked. NHS England advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for black or dark red poo or bloody diarrhoea. It advises calling 999 or going to A&E for bleeding from the bottom that will not stop, or a large amount of blood or clots. A GP appointment is the usual route for other symptoms.

sections.heading: How is bowel cancer staged?
sections.body:
Bowel cancer is the term for colon cancer and rectal cancer, and treatment differs between the two. Doctors usually describe how far the cancer has spread using the TNM system. T describes the main tumour, N whether nearby lymph nodes are involved, and M whether the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.

Macmillan describes number stages from 0 to 4, although some providers list only stages 1 to 4. Stage 0 means the cancer is confined to the mucosa, the innermost layer of the bowel wall. Stage 3 means the cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread elsewhere. Stage 4 means it has spread to distant organs such as the liver or lungs, or to the lining of the abdomen called the peritoneum.

sections.heading: What happens at the GP and in hospital?
sections.body:
The NHS and Bowel Cancer UK describe a GP asking when symptoms started, whether they come and go, and about general health, medical history and any family history of bowel cancer. The doctor may feel the tummy and ask to do a rectal examination, where a gloved finger is placed inside the back passage to feel for lumps. The NHS says this can be uncomfortable but should not be painful, and a person can ask for someone else to be in the room. The GP may give a home test kit called a FIT, which checks for hidden blood in the poo, and may arrange a blood test.

Cancer Research UK says an urgent referral means a hospital appointment or more tests within two weeks, and that it does not definitely mean cancer. Macmillan calls colonoscopy the main test used to diagnose bowel cancer. Polyps found during it can be removed, and biopsies (small samples) can be taken. CT colonography is used if a colonoscopy did not give clear enough pictures.

sections.heading: How is bowel cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says people may be offered a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and targeted medicines, depending on the details of the cancer. NHS hospital trust pages add that the size and location of the cancer matter, along with general health, age, and the grade, stage and type of cancer.

Removing the affected section of bowel is the core treatment. NHS 111 Wales says surgery is usually able to completely remove cancer that is confined to the bowel, and that a local resection may be enough for very small, early tumours. Chemotherapy can be given before surgery to shrink a tumour, after surgery to lower the risk of the cancer coming back, or to treat advanced cancer. Targeted medicines and immunotherapy are sometimes used for advanced bowel cancer.

Radiotherapy is used mostly for rectal cancer. It is often combined with chemotherapy, called chemoradiotherapy, and is usually given before surgery.

sections.heading: What is a stoma?
sections.body:
A stoma is an opening made on the tummy so that waste can leave the body and collect in a bag. A colostomy is made from the colon, and an ileostomy from the small bowel. A surgeon may make a temporary stoma to let the bowel heal after surgery. Reversal usually takes place after treatment, and further treatment such as chemotherapy may delay it.

Macmillan says only a small number of people with colon cancer need a permanent stoma. If a rectal cancer is very low and close to the anus, a permanent stoma is more likely. Colostomy UK says people with a colostomy should not generally have a high stoma output. NHS trust leaflets on ileostomies list dry mouth with constant thirst, dizzy spells and passing less urine as signs of dehydration.

sections.heading: What can happen after treatment?
sections.body:
Some people develop low anterior resection syndrome after an operation that removes all or part of the rectum. Macmillan says bowel changes can often be managed by changing the diet. A review describes symptoms such as urgency, frequent bowel movements, clustering of stools and difficulty emptying.

Macmillan says tiredness can continue for weeks or months after treatment finishes. It describes late effects as effects that begin months or even years later. Bowel Cancer UK lists bowel and bladder changes among them and says healthcare teams are used to talking about effects on sex life. The NICE guideline says follow-up after surgery for non-metastatic disease should include a blood test for carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) and a CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

faqs.q: Does a bowel cancer symptom always mean cancer?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says having these symptoms does not definitely mean bowel cancer, but it is important to get checked by a GP. Many symptoms have other causes, such as piles, infections or inflammatory bowel disease. An urgent referral to a specialist also does not definitely mean cancer.

faqs.q: Is a colonoscopy done under sedation?
faqs.a: NHS trust leaflets describe sedation, or gas and air (Entonox) as an alternative. Entonox is a gas the person breathes in themselves, and it wears off faster. Trusts give the test as taking about 20 minutes to an hour, longer if a polyp is removed.

faqs.q: Will I need a stoma?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Macmillan says only a small number of people with colon cancer need a permanent stoma. A surgeon may make a temporary stoma to let the bowel heal after surgery, and reversal usually takes place after treatment. A permanent stoma is more likely when a rectal cancer is very low and close to the anus.

faqs.q: Which bleeding needs urgent help?
faqs.a: NHS England advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for black or dark red poo or bloody diarrhoea. It advises calling 999 or going to A&E for bleeding from the bottom that will not stop, or a large amount of blood or clots.

cirrhosis.name: Cirrhosis
cirrhosis.definition: Scarring of the liver from long-term damage, in which nodules of regenerating cells are surrounded by fibrous bands that distort blood flow and impair function.
cirrhosis.overview: Years of injury from alcohol, fatty liver disease or viral hepatitis replace liver tissue with scar. The result is failure of the liver's jobs (jaundice, bleeding, confusion) and high pressure in the portal vein (varices, fluid in the abdomen, an enlarged spleen). Stopping or treating the cause can slow or halt further scarring and may allow some recovery, but complications and the risk of liver cancer can persist, so follow-up continues. Cirrhosis is the final stage of chronic liver disease: scar tissue replaces healthy tissue and stops the liver working normally. Early on it often causes nothing noticeable, and it is sometimes found by chance on an abdominal ultrasound or on blood tests taken for another reason. As it progresses people report fatigue, itchy skin, poor appetite, unintended weight loss and swelling of the legs and ankles, then fluid in the abdomen (ascites) and yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice). Hepatic encephalopathy, confusion caused by the failing liver no longer clearing toxins, can progress to unconsciousness. Some people have more than one cause at the same time, for example alcohol and fatty liver disease.
causes: Alcohol
Metabolic dysfunction-associated (fatty) liver disease
Hepatitis B and C
Autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis
Haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Some medicines (drug-induced liver injury)
More than one cause acting together
riskFactors: Unprotected sex or injected drug use (viral hepatitis)
signs: Jaundice, spider naevi, red palms
Enlarged spleen, ascites
Muscle wasting, bruising
Confusion and a flapping tremor (encephalopathy)
Oedema of the legs and ankles
Itching and scratch marks
complications: Bleeding oesophageal varices
Ascites and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Hepatic encephalopathy
Liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma)
Kidney failure (hepatorenal syndrome)
Malnutrition, weight loss and muscle wasting
cirrhosis.diagnosis: Liver function tests, clotting and platelet count; ultrasound or elastography (FibroScan) measuring stiffness; tests for the cause (hepatitis viruses, iron, autoantibodies); endoscopy for varices; six-monthly ultrasound for cancer surveillance. The diagnosis rests on history, examination and test results together: blood tests show liver damage, reduced synthetic function and infection; imaging shows a nodular liver, an enlarged spleen and ascites; elastography measures stiffness without a needle, so liver biopsy is reserved for cases where the cause or stage remains uncertain.
cirrhosis.treatment: Remove the cause: complete abstinence from alcohol, weight loss, antivirals for hepatitis B and C. Diuretics for ascites, beta blockers or banding for varices, lactulose for encephalopathy, nutrition, vaccination. Liver transplantation for decompensated disease. No treatment reverses established cirrhosis, but treating the disease that caused it may stop it getting worse and prevent liver failure: antiviral medicines for hepatitis B and C, steroid medicines for autoimmune hepatitis, abstinence for alcohol-related disease and weight loss for fatty liver disease. Complications are managed as they arise with medicines for abdominal and leg swelling, for encephalopathy and for dilated oesophageal veins, and with surveillance imaging for liver cancer. Vaccination protects against hepatitis B, one of the leading causes. Liver transplantation is considered for advanced, decompensated disease.
cirrhosis.prevention: Drink within recommended limits or not at all, keep a healthy weight, vaccinate against hepatitis B, never share needles, treat hepatitis C. Hepatitis B vaccination prevents one of the leading causes outright.
cirrhosis.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, confusion or drowsiness, a rapidly swelling abdomen with fever, or deepening jaundice. MedlinePlus advises emergency help for sudden abdominal or chest pain in someone with cirrhosis, and prompt contact with a clinician for any new symptom suggesting the disease.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.definition: Inflammation of the pancreas, acute when its own enzymes are activated inside the gland, chronic when repeated injury leads to scarring and loss of function.
pancreatitis.overview: Gallstones and alcohol cause four in five cases of acute pancreatitis. Activated enzymes digest the gland and surrounding fat, and severe cases trigger a body-wide inflammatory response with organ failure. Most attacks are mild and settle in days; chronic pancreatitis causes lasting pain, malabsorption and diabetes. Acute pancreatitis is short-term and often resolves within days with treatment; chronic pancreatitis worsens over time, causes lasting damage and can follow one or more acute attacks. In an acute attack, upper abdominal pain spreads to the back with nausea and vomiting; fever and a fast pulse are common and, in severe cases, blood pressure falls, dehydration develops and organ failure, internal bleeding or death can follow. Chronic disease presents differently, with nausea, weight loss and oily stools, because digestive enzymes such as trypsin no longer reach the gut in adequate amounts. A gallstone lodging in the common bile duct blocks pancreatic drainage; alcohol is the leading cause of chronic disease.
causes: Gallstones blocking the duct
Alcohol
High triglycerides, high calcium
Some drugs (azathioprine, valproate, thiazides)
After ERCP
Viral infections, trauma, genetic mutations
Cystic fibrosis and other inherited disorders
Autoimmune pancreatitis
Injury or surgery to the pancreas; infections such as mumps; lupus
signs: Severe epigastric tenderness
Fast pulse, low blood pressure in severe disease
Bruising of the flanks or around the navel in haemorrhagic cases
Jaundice with a duct stone
Dehydration
Weight loss and oily stools in chronic disease
complications: Pancreatic necrosis and infection
Pseudocysts
Organ failure and death in severe attacks
Diabetes and malabsorption in chronic disease
Pancreatic cancer risk in chronic pancreatitis
Internal bleeding in severe attacks
Dehydration and low blood pressure
pancreatitis.diagnosis: Typical pain with a serum lipase or amylase more than three times normal; ultrasound for gallstones; CT after 48 to 72 hours if severe to assess necrosis; blood tests to score severity. In NHS practice acute pancreatitis is usually diagnosed from blood tests, with a CT scan in some cases, and further tests are then run to identify the underlying cause so it can be treated.
pancreatitis.treatment: Intravenous fluids, pain relief, early feeding when tolerated; ERCP to remove a duct stone with cholangitis; antibiotics and drainage for infected necrosis; cholecystectomy before discharge for gallstone pancreatitis. Chronic disease: stop alcohol and smoking, enzyme supplements, pain management, diabetes care. Treatment in hospital includes fluids given into a vein, nutritional support, painkillers, and antibiotics if an infection develops; most people start to improve within a week. Early feeding is favoured because early enteral nutrition has been shown to improve outcomes. For gallstone pancreatitis the gallbladder is removed during the same admission or soon afterwards to limit the risk of recurrence; alcohol-related disease improves with stopping alcohol and treatment for dependency. Surgery is reserved for complications.
pancreatitis.prevention: Moderate alcohol, treat gallstones once symptomatic, control triglycerides, stop smoking.
pancreatitis.seekCare: Emergency care for severe constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting, especially after alcohol or with known gallstones.

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.definition: The commonest joint disease: progressive loss of articular cartilage with changes in the underlying bone, causing pain and stiffness, most often in the knees, hips, hands and spine.
osteoarthritis.overview: Osteoarthritis is not simply wear: it is a failed repair process in which cartilage thins, bone thickens and forms spurs (osteophytes), and the joint lining becomes intermittently inflamed. Pain builds over years, worse with use and at the end of the day. It affects most people over 65 to some degree. Pain and stiffness are the hallmark. Early on, symptoms may appear only after exercise, but over time they can become constant, and they often come and go in episodes related to activity levels and even the weather. Swelling, a reduced range of motion and weakness or wasting of the muscles around the joint also occur. The joints most often affected are those near the ends of the fingers, the base of the thumb, the neck, the lower back, the knees and the hips. The disease is thought to stem from mechanical stress on the joint combined with low-grade inflammation, and the problems usually come on over years.
causes: Mechanical load on a susceptible joint: age, previous injury, malalignment, obesity
Genetic factors, especially in hand OA
Abnormal development or alignment of the joint or limb
riskFactors: Heavy manual work or elite sport
signs: Bony enlargement, crepitus, reduced range of motion
Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes on the fingers
Effusion in a flared knee
Antalgic gait
Weakness or wasting of the muscles around the affected joint
complications: Disability and loss of independence
Falls
Chronic pain and depression
osteoarthritis.diagnosis: Clinical in a person over 45 with activity-related pain and brief morning stiffness. X-rays show joint-space narrowing, sclerosis and osteophytes but correlate poorly with symptoms; blood tests are normal and are used to exclude inflammatory arthritis. Early joint damage does not usually show on X-ray. MRI shows soft-tissue damage and is especially useful when a joint locks or gives way. Blood tests and joint-fluid sampling are used to rule out other causes such as infection or gout rather than to confirm osteoarthritis.
osteoarthritis.treatment: Exercise and strengthening, weight loss, education and pacing are the core treatments. Topical NSAIDs, paracetamol and oral NSAIDs for pain; walking aids and braces; steroid injections for flares. Joint replacement when pain limits life despite these. There is no cure. The NHS describes three main strands: lifestyle measures, medicines to relieve pain, and supportive therapies that make everyday activities easier; surgery is considered only in some cases where other treatments have not helped. Regular exercise that keeps a person active, builds up muscle and strengthens the joints usually improves symptoms. NIAMS advises starting slowly with a plan from a doctor or physiotherapist that combines range-of-motion and stretching work with strengthening using weights or resistance bands, to reduce pain and stiffness and increase flexibility, strength and endurance.
osteoarthritis.prevention: Healthy weight, regular low-impact exercise, strong muscles around the joints, and avoiding joint injury.
osteoarthritis.seekCare: See a doctor for joint pain limiting daily activities; urgent care for a hot, red, swollen joint with fever.

sections.heading: What does osteoarthritis feel like, and does it get worse?
sections.body:
Pain and stiffness in the affected joints are the main features of osteoarthritis. NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing once a person starts to move. Versus Arthritis says a short spell of stiffness after rest is common.

The knees, hips and small joints of the hands are the most common areas affected, and the big toes and feet can also be involved.

The NHS says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time. Symptoms vary from person to person and between different joints, and in more severe cases they can be continuous. Some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms at all.

sections.heading: How is osteoarthritis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP or other healthcare professional asks about the symptoms and examines the joints. NHS inform says there is no single definitive test for osteoarthritis. A NICE draft evidence review says that, without features pointing to another problem, osteoarthritis can be diagnosed through history and examination alone.

NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage there is. For the hip and knee, an X-ray is sometimes used to help the diagnosis. Versus Arthritis says doctors rarely use an X-ray or blood test for knee problems, mainly to rule out other causes. MedlinePlus notes that X-rays may show loss of joint space and bone spurs, and that some people who have these changes have no symptoms.

MedlinePlus says blood tests do not help diagnose osteoarthritis, but they can check for other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout. NHS inform lists joint pain, tenderness, stiffness, swelling and restricted movement as reasons to contact a GP practice.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for osteoarthritis?
sections.body:
The NHS says osteoarthritis cannot be cured but that a number of treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. NICE guidance calls therapeutic exercise and weight management core treatments, and NHS inform describes keeping the joint active and strengthening the muscles around it as the best way to manage symptoms.

For pain, the NHS describes creams containing an anti-inflammatory medicine (topical NSAIDs) as often used for the knees and hands, and NICE advises offering one for knee osteoarthritis. Capsaicin cream is another option, and burning is its most common side effect. The NHS describes paracetamol as suitable for short-term use. NSAID tablets are generally considered if creams do not help, and because they can wear down the stomach lining, a medicine that reduces stomach acid may be given alongside them. Opioids such as codeine are generally limited to short-term use because of their side effects.

Steroid injections are sometimes offered when other treatments have not worked, and the NHS says they can ease pain for several weeks or months. NICE says to consider a corticosteroid injection into the joint when other medicines are ineffective or unsuitable.

sections.heading: What can help with osteoarthritis day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says supportive aids such as shock-absorbing footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks can reduce strain on the joints during everyday activities. Patient leaflets from NHS services describe pacing, which means balancing rest and activity, and note that taking on too much on a low-pain day can lead to worse pain afterwards. Supportive shoes are described as improving comfort and balance, and a walking stick can take pressure off an affected hip.

The leaflets describe heat as often suggested for stiffness or aching and cold for a sudden flare-up or swelling, with packs wrapped in a cloth. A physiotherapist can help build a plan guided by a person's symptoms, physical function and goals.

The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin supplements on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work.

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body:
NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. It may greatly improve symptoms, but it cannot be guaranteed to resolve them fully. Versus Arthritis describes lifestyle changes, medication, therapies and, rarely, surgery as the ways to help.

MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. The operations it lists include trimming damaged cartilage through a keyhole procedure (arthroscopy), realigning bone (osteotomy), fusing a joint, and partial or total joint replacement. NHS inform says joint replacement is the most common surgical option and that the decision is made with an orthopaedic surgeon, a doctor who specialises in bone and joint surgery.

faqs.q: Can osteoarthritis be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. The NHS also says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time, and symptoms vary from person to person. NICE guidance describes therapeutic exercise and weight management as core treatments.

faqs.q: Is an X-ray needed to diagnose osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage is present. A GP asks about the symptoms and examines the joints, and there is no single definitive test. MedlinePlus notes that some people who have X-ray changes have no symptoms. Blood tests are used to look for other conditions, not to confirm osteoarthritis.

faqs.q: Do osteoarthritis symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing with movement. Severity varies between people and between joints, and some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms.

faqs.q: Do glucosamine and chondroitin supplements help?
faqs.a: The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work. The options the NHS does describe are lifestyle measures, pain medication such as creams, and supportive therapies and aids such as footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks.

faqs.q: Does everyone with osteoarthritis need surgery?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. When surgery is considered, the options include fusing a joint and partial or total joint replacement, decided with an orthopaedic surgeon.

rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid-arthritis.definition: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial lining of joints, causing symmetrical inflammation that can destroy cartilage and bone.
rheumatoid-arthritis.overview: Rheumatoid arthritis typically starts in the small joints of the hands and feet with prolonged morning stiffness and swelling, and can involve the eyes, lungs, heart and blood vessels. Untreated it deforms and disables; started early, disease-modifying drugs now prevent most damage. Arthritis is the cardinal feature, but extra-articular disease is common: interstitial lung disease is among the most frequent manifestations and is more likely in smokers, in men and in people positive for anti-CCP antibodies and rheumatoid factor. Treatment with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) is recommended early for every patient because it slows joint destruction and prevents deformity, although these medicines carry considerable side effects and cost.
causes: Autoimmunity against citrullinated proteins, in genetically susceptible people, often triggered by smoking or infection
riskFactors: Smoking, male sex and antibody positivity raise the risk of lung involvement
signs: Symmetrical swelling of metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints
Morning stiffness over an hour
Rheumatoid nodules
Later: ulnar deviation, swan-neck deformities
complications: Joint destruction and deformity
Cardiovascular disease
Lung fibrosis, pleural disease
Anaemia, osteoporosis
Cervical spine instability (atlanto-axial subluxation)
Interstitial lung disease, the most common form of lung involvement
Drug toxicity: marrow suppression, infection, liver damage and pneumonitis with methotrexate
rheumatoid-arthritis.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, raised CRP and ESR, and ultrasound or X-ray showing synovitis and erosions. Early referral to rheumatology within weeks changes outcomes. Lung involvement is diagnosed from clinical and radiological findings, and pulmonary function tests may show a restrictive pattern.
rheumatoid-arthritis.treatment: Methotrexate started early, with short-term steroids to control symptoms; biologic drugs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6, B-cell depletion) or JAK inhibitors if disease stays active; NSAIDs for pain; physiotherapy, occupational therapy and cardiovascular risk management. Methotrexate is the most commonly used DMARD, with leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine as alternatives; it reduces pain and X-ray joint damage, but a substantial minority of patients do not respond well despite optimal dosing. DMARDs fall into three groups: conventional synthetic (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine), targeted synthetic (JAK inhibitors) and biologic (TNF and IL-6 inhibitors). Methotrexate can suppress the bone marrow and cause serious infections, liver damage, mouth and skin problems and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. NSAIDs reduce swelling and pain well but do not prevent joint damage, so they are used for short periods at low doses alongside a DMARD.
rheumatoid-arthritis.prevention: Not smoking and good dental health reduce risk; early treatment prevents damage.
rheumatoid-arthritis.seekCare: See a doctor within weeks for swelling of several joints with morning stiffness; urgent care for a single hot joint with fever or new neck pain with tingling in the arms.

sections.heading: What does rheumatoid arthritis feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes rheumatoid arthritis (RA) as a long-term condition that causes pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints. It commonly involves the hands, wrists and feet, and the small joints of the hands and feet are often affected first. Joint pain, swelling and stiffness are the core symptoms. Stiffness is often worse in the morning or after rest, and it usually lasts longer than the stiffness seen in osteoarthritis.

Inflamed joints can swell and feel warm and tender, and firm lumps called rheumatoid nodules sometimes form under the skin. Symptoms most often begin slowly over weeks to a few months. Some people also have general symptoms, including tiredness, fever, sweating, poor appetite and weight loss. Inflammation can also affect the eyes, causing dryness, or the heart and lungs, causing chest pain. Symptoms vary between people and can come and go.

sections.heading: What is a flare-up and what can help?
sections.body:
Symptoms can come back or get worse, which is known as a flare-up. One NHS trust lists stopping or winding down treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and poor sleep as causes of flares.

Guidance broadly describes heat as easing stiffness and cold as easing swelling, and sources stress placing a towel between the skin and the heat or cold source. Sources recommend gentle movement rather than rest alone. NRAS, a rheumatoid arthritis charity, says exercise is important because it helps reduce the risk of further joint damage. NRAS advises speaking to the rheumatology team about regular flares, or a flare that is not going down with self-management. A Worcestershire hospital trust adds that recurrent flares can show that a change to treatment is needed.

sections.heading: How is rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed?
sections.body:
Rheumatoid arthritis can be difficult to diagnose because many conditions cause joint stiffness and inflammation, and there is no definitive test for it. The NHS advises seeing a GP if these symptoms appear. The GP carries out a physical examination, checking the joints for swelling and how easily they move. If the GP thinks the person has rheumatoid arthritis, they refer them to a specialist called a rheumatologist.

Blood tests include ESR and CRP for inflammation, a full blood count, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP. People who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everybody with the condition has this antibody. A Manchester guide for GPs notes that a negative result does not exclude the condition and a positive result does not equate to a diagnosis. X-rays and MRI scans may be used to check for joint inflammation and damage, and ultrasound is used in some early arthritis clinics. Seropositive means these antibodies are found in the blood, and seronegative means they are not.

sections.heading: What medicines are used to treat it?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatments can help reduce inflammation in the joints, relieve pain, prevent or slow down joint damage, reduce disability and enable people to be as active as possible. Care usually involves the GP and several specialists. The disease-modifying medicines fall into two main groups, disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biological treatments.

Initial treatment is usually a combination of DMARD tablets, and methotrexate is usually the first medicine given. Biological treatments are generally used alongside methotrexate or another DMARD, typically when DMARDs alone have not worked. JAK inhibitors are offered to adults with moderate to severe disease who cannot take DMARDs or biological treatments, or who found them ineffective. Steroids can be given as tablets or injections and are usually used for short periods. The NHS says long-term steroid use can have serious side effects.

sections.heading: Monitoring and supportive care
sections.body:
The NHS says methotrexate can affect blood cells and the liver, so regular blood tests are used to monitor this. MedlinePlus says DMARDs may have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are needed. MedlinePlus also says corticosteroids work very well to reduce joint swelling and inflammation, but they can have long-term side effects and do not prevent joint damage if used alone.

NHS inform lists physiotherapy, which helps improve muscle strength, flexibility and fitness. If the condition causes problems with everyday tasks, occupational therapy may help, and an occupational therapist can provide training and advice to protect the joints at home and at work. A support for the joints, such as a splint, may also be recommended.

sections.heading: Surgery and outlook
sections.body:
The NHS says surgery may be needed to improve joint movement, reduce pain or correct joint damage, and some people need a hip, knee or shoulder joint replaced. NHS inform lists hand and wrist surgery and arthroscopy among the options. The NHS notes that some function may not be restored after a damaged joint is replaced by a prosthetic one.

NHS inform says there is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis, but with treatment symptoms such as joint pain, swelling and stiffness improve. Other NHS sites agree that early treatment reduces the risk of joint damage. One review says rheumatoid nodules in the lung are usually symptom-free and often resolve on their own. One source says clinical remission is reached and sustained in a minority of people, and that drug-free remission remains rare.

faqs.q: Can rheumatoid arthritis be cured?
faqs.a: NHS inform says there is no cure for rheumatoid arthritis, but with treatment symptoms such as joint pain, swelling and stiffness improve. The NHS says treatments can help reduce inflammation, relieve pain, prevent or slow down joint damage and reduce disability. One source says clinical remission is reached and sustained in a minority of people, and drug-free remission remains rare.

faqs.q: What does seropositive rheumatoid arthritis mean?
faqs.a: Seropositive means rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies are found in the blood, and seronegative means they are not. People who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everybody with the condition has this antibody.

faqs.q: Why are regular blood tests needed during treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says methotrexate can affect blood cells and the liver, so regular blood tests monitor this. MedlinePlus says DMARDs may have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are needed. One NHS trust leaflet says hydroxychloroquine does not need blood monitoring checks, although people taking it still have regular checks for other reasons.

faqs.q: Does rheumatoid arthritis only affect the joints?
faqs.a: Joints are the main target, but the NHS lists general symptoms that can occur, including tiredness, fever, sweating, poor appetite and weight loss. It says inflammation can also affect the eyes, causing dryness, or the heart and lungs, causing chest pain.

faqs.q: Does everyone with rheumatoid arthritis need surgery?
faqs.a: The NHS says surgery may be needed to improve joint movement, reduce pain or correct joint damage, and some people need a hip, knee or shoulder joint replaced. NHS inform describes surgery as sometimes needed, alongside medicines, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, so it is not described as needed by everyone.

faqs.q: What can trigger a flare?
faqs.a: One NHS trust lists stopping or winding down treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and poor sleep. Another source notes that a flare is often the result of several factors building up together. NRAS advises speaking to the rheumatology team about regular flares, or a flare that is not going down with self-management.

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.definition: Loss of bone mass and deterioration of bone architecture that makes bones fragile and prone to fracture after minimal trauma.
osteoporosis.overview: Bone is constantly remodelled; after the peak mass reached around 30, resorption slowly outpaces formation, sharply so in women after the menopause. Osteoporosis is silent until a bone breaks: the wrist, spine or hip. Hip fractures in older adults carry a high risk of death and loss of independence, and are largely preventable. It is the major cause of fractures in postmenopausal women and in older men, and is often called a silent disease: there are no symptoms until a bone breaks, so it is frequently diagnosed only when a fall or sudden impact causes a fracture. Weakened bone may also break during ordinary activities such as bending, lifting or even coughing. When the spine is involved, height is lost and a stooped posture develops. If the diet does not supply enough calcium the body takes it from bone, and sometimes bone loss occurs without any identifiable cause or simply runs in families.
causes: Oestrogen loss at the menopause
Ageing
Long-term steroid treatment
Low calcium and vitamin D, malabsorption
Overactive thyroid or parathyroid, low testosterone
Immobility
Chronic conditions and medicines other than steroids; sometimes no cause is found
riskFactors: Female sex, early menopause, or long gaps in sex-hormone exposure (including after removal of the ovaries or testes)
Thin bones running in the family
signs: Loss of height, stooped posture (kyphosis)
Fragility fracture after a fall from standing height
Fracture from an everyday stress such as bending, lifting or coughing
complications: Hip, vertebral and wrist fractures
Chronic back pain
Loss of independence
osteoporosis.diagnosis: DXA bone density scan (a T-score of −2.5 or lower), fracture risk calculators (FRAX), spine X-ray for vertebral fractures, and blood tests for vitamin D, calcium, thyroid and other secondary causes. Bone mineral density is measured non-invasively by DXA at the hip and spine, which NIAMS describes as the most common test for measuring bone density, used to diagnose osteoporosis, predict fracture risk and monitor treatment; a heel ultrasound can screen for bone loss but a DXA scan is still needed for the diagnosis. Clinicians also weigh fracture history, lifestyle, medical history and medicines, and may estimate future fracture risk with an online tool such as FRAX or QFracture. Screening is directed at older women and at younger women with additional risk factors.
osteoporosis.treatment: Calcium and vitamin D sufficiency, weight-bearing and balance exercise, fall prevention; bisphosphonates (alendronate) first line, denosumab or teriparatide for severe disease; treat secondary causes. Treatment combines lifestyle change (diet, exercise, fall prevention and cutting back on tobacco and alcohol) and calcium and vitamin D supplements with medication. Bisphosphonates are the main medicines used to prevent and treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women; denosumab lessens bone loss and increases bone density. When osteoporosis comes from another condition or a medicine, the prescriber reviews the cause and whether the medicine is still needed (a medicine is never stopped or changed without their advice), and bone-protective treatment is often started at the same time.
osteoporosis.prevention: Build peak bone mass with exercise and calcium in youth, keep active, do not smoke, limit alcohol, ensure vitamin D, review medicines that cause falls or bone loss.
osteoporosis.seekCare: Any fracture from a minor fall after 50, sudden back pain in an older person, or loss of more than 4 cm in height should prompt assessment.

sections.heading: What does osteoporosis feel like?
sections.body:
Osteoporosis usually causes no symptoms until a bone breaks. NIAMS describes it as a silent disease, because people may not know they have it until a bone breaks. NHS 111 Wales says it is not usually painful until a bone is broken, although broken bones in the spine are a common cause of long-term pain.

The hip, spine and wrist are the usual places for fractures. A bone broken after a minor fall or injury is known as a fragility fracture, because a healthy bone would usually survive the same fall. Spinal fractures can be silent, and a person may not always be aware that one has happened. The NHS 111 Wales entry adds that a cough or sneeze can sometimes partly collapse a spinal bone.

Warning signs of a spinal fracture include severe back pain, loss of height, or a stooped or hunched posture. Some sources say a weakened vertebra may fracture even without a fall or significant force.

sections.heading: How is osteoporosis diagnosed, and what is a bone scan like?
sections.body:
A bone density scan, also called a DEXA or DXA scan, uses low-dose X-rays to see how dense, or strong, the bones are. MedlinePlus describes it as painless, and notes that a person receives more radiation from a chest X-ray than from a DEXA scan. For the central scan, the person lies on a soft table while the scanner passes over the lower spine and hip, and must stay still.

MedlinePlus says people may be told to stop calcium supplements before the test, and the timing varies between sources and facilities. People may eat and drink as normal and continue their usual prescription medicines.

NHS 111 Wales says the result is usually used alongside a fracture risk assessment. Treatment depends on factors such as age, sex, fracture risk and previous injuries, not on the scan result alone. One research review notes that bone density is a continuous risk factor for fracture, with no natural threshold, and that scores overlap between people who do and do not fracture.

sections.heading: How is osteoporosis treated, and what are the side effects?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales suggests regular exercise, a diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, and fall-prevention steps at home. For medicines, it lists the bisphosphonates alendronic acid, risedronic acid, ibandronic acid and zoledronic acid, which work by slowing bone breakdown.

Other medicines exist. Versus Arthritis says denosumab is recommended for postmenopausal women who cannot take bisphosphonates, and the NHS says it may be recommended if other medicines cannot be taken or osteoporosis is severe. Teriparatide, a bone-building medicine, is generally positioned for severe osteoporosis at high risk of further fracture, according to NHS guidance for primary care.

Side effects of bisphosphonates can include irritation of the gullet, according to NHS 111 Wales, which also says osteonecrosis of the jaw, a problem with the jaw bone, is rare. Research reviews report that the risk of an unusual thigh bone fracture, called an atypical femoral fracture, rises with the length of bisphosphonate treatment, although absolute risks are small. A task force report from the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research suggests periodic reassessment of treatment.

sections.heading: Living with osteoporosis: exercise, food and avoiding falls
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis says weight-bearing exercise is good for maintaining bone strength and reducing the risk of osteoporosis. It adds that vitamin D is needed for the body to absorb and process calcium. The NHS describes weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening activities as the strongest options for bone strength, with walking, hiking and dancing as examples. MedlinePlus lists balance training, which can include tai chi and yoga, alongside weight-bearing activity and resistance work.

MedlinePlus advises avoiding exercise that carries a risk of falling and high-impact exercise that could cause fractures in older adults.

NHS 111 Wales suggests a diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, stopping smoking and cutting down alcohol, and fall-prevention steps at home. MedlinePlus examples include removing throw rugs, adding grab bars and non-slip flooring in bathrooms, leaving night lights on, and wearing low-heeled, well-fitting shoes, including slippers.

sections.heading: Why do the menopause, medicines and lifestyle affect bone?
sections.body:
The NHS says women are more at risk than men because hormone changes at the menopause directly affect bone density, and describes oestrogen as essential for healthy bones. It also lists an early menopause as a risk factor.

Versus Arthritis lists steroids, especially those taken by mouth, as a risk factor,. NIAMS notes that some cancer medicines and glucocorticoid steroids may increase the risk.

NIAMS calls chronic heavy drinking a significant risk factor and says smoking is a risk factor for osteoporosis and fracture. It adds that researchers are still studying whether the effect of smoking comes from tobacco use alone or because people who smoke have more risk factors. NIAMS also notes that the risk may increase if a parent has a history of osteoporosis or hip fracture.

sections.heading: Where does care for a fracture start?
sections.body:
A suspected hip fracture should go to an Emergency Department rather than a minor injury unit, according to an NHS referral document. In an emergency, such as a suspected hip fracture or a severe injury, the UK emergency number is 999.

A patient leaflet on spinal fractures says people with serious symptoms should go to the nearest Emergency Department immediately by ambulance, and move as little as possible until seen there. For most spinal fractures, follow-up is usually with the GP, and painkillers and mobility advice come from there.

The NHS 111 Wales entry names the Royal Osteoporosis Society as the UK charity with more detailed information about the condition.

faqs.q: Can osteoporosis cause symptoms before a bone breaks?
faqs.a: Osteoporosis usually causes no symptoms until a bone breaks, and the break often follows a minor fall. Warning signs of a spinal fracture include severe back pain, loss of height, or a stooped or hunched posture. Follow-up for spinal fractures is usually with the GP, while a suspected hip fracture goes to an Emergency Department (A&E); in an emergency the UK number is 999.

faqs.q: Does a bone density scan hurt?
faqs.a: A DEXA scan is described as painless and uses a low dose of X-ray. For the central scan, the person lies on a soft table while the scanner passes over the lower spine and hip, and stays still. MedlinePlus notes that a chest X-ray gives more radiation than a DEXA scan.

faqs.q: Why are women affected more often than men?
faqs.a: The NHS says women are more at risk because hormone changes at the menopause directly affect bone density, and oestrogen is essential for healthy bones. Other risk factors named by NIAMS include glucocorticoid steroids, chronic heavy drinking, smoking and a parent with a history of osteoporosis or hip fracture.

faqs.q: Is exercise good for people with osteoporosis?
faqs.a: The NHS describes weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening activities as the strongest options for bone strength, with walking, hiking and dancing as examples. MedlinePlus lists balance training, which can include tai chi and yoga. MedlinePlus also advises avoiding exercise that carries a risk of falling and high-impact exercise that could cause fractures in older adults.

faqs.q: Do osteoporosis medicines have side effects?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says bisphosphonate side effects can include irritation of the gullet, and that osteonecrosis of the jaw is rare. Research reviews report that the risk of an unusual thigh bone fracture rises with the length of treatment, although absolute risks are small. A task force report suggests periodic reassessment of treatment.

fracture.name: Bone fracture
fracture.definition: A break in the continuity of a bone, from a hairline crack to a shattered, displaced or open injury.
fracture.overview: Bones break when the force exceeds their strength: a fall on the outstretched hand fractures the wrist, a twist the ankle, a car crash the femur. In weakened bone (osteoporosis, cancer) a minor force is enough. Bone heals by forming a callus that is remodelled over months; the aim of treatment is to hold the fragments in a good position while it does. Symptoms vary with the bone involved: intense pain, a limb that looks out of place, swelling and tenderness, bruising and difficulty moving the part are typical, and some people feel a snap or grinding at the moment of injury. A simple crack may cause little pain, so a break is not always obvious. Healing takes weeks for minor fractures and months for severe ones, with the surrounding soft tissues often taking longer to recover than the bone itself; smoking and diabetes slow the process.
causes: Trauma: falls, sport, road accidents, assaults
Repeated stress (stress fractures in runners and soldiers)
Weakened bone: osteoporosis, tumours, infection
riskFactors: Poor balance, medicines that cause falls
signs: Pain, swelling, bruising, deformity
Inability to bear weight or use the limb
Crepitus
Open wound over the bone in open fractures
A snap or grinding sensation reported at the time of injury
Numbness or tingling below the injury, a warning sign of nerve or vessel damage
complications: Damage to nerves and vessels
Compartment syndrome
Infection in open fractures
Non-union or malunion
Fat embolism, DVT
Post-traumatic osteoarthritis
Delayed healing, prolonged by smoking and diabetes
fracture.diagnosis: X-rays in two views; CT for complex joint, spine and pelvic fractures; MRI for occult fractures such as the scaphoid or stress fractures; assessment of circulation and nerves beyond the break. X-rays are the usual way to confirm a fracture and judge its position and severity, though it can be hard to tell clinically whether a bone is broken, so imaging is needed for most suspected breaks. CT shows the detail of complex joint, spine and pelvic fractures, and MRI shows soft tissues, bone bruising and stress fractures that X-rays miss.
fracture.treatment: Realign (reduce) if displaced, then hold: a cast or splint for stable fractures, or surgery with plates, screws, nails or external fixation for unstable ones. Pain relief, elevation, early movement of neighbouring joints, and physiotherapy. Open fractures need urgent cleaning and antibiotics. The common approach is immobilisation: a cast or splint keeps the bone from moving while it heals. Surgery is used when the bone needs realigning or holding, with metal rods, screws or plates securing the fragments. Open fractures, where the bone has broken the skin, need urgent surgery to remove debris, clean the wound and cut away unhealthy tissue, with antibiotics against infection. Pain relief and anti-inflammatory medicines are used, and physiotherapy afterwards restores movement, strength and function. Until help arrives, first aid is to keep the person still and calm, not to move the injured part or try to line up the bone, and to use ice and elevation for swelling.
fracture.prevention: Fall prevention and bone health in older adults, protective equipment in sport, road safety, treating osteoporosis. A balanced diet, hydration, avoiding smoking and heavy alcohol use, and following advice on when to bear weight support healing after a fracture.
fracture.seekCare: Emergency care for deformity, a bone through the skin, numbness or a cold pale limb, or a suspected hip, spine or pelvic fracture; same-day care for any inability to bear weight or use a limb after injury. Compartment syndrome, a rare but serious rise in pressure within the muscle compartments, most often develops in the first days after a fracture and causes sudden, intense pain and swelling; it needs emergency care. Redness, warmth, pus or fever around a wound suggest infection, particularly after an open fracture.
