acl-injury.name: ACL injury
acl-injury.definition: A sprain or tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, the band inside the knee that stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and controls rotation.
acl-injury.overview: ACL tears happen in a moment: a pivot, a sudden stop or a landing with the knee twisted inward, often with a pop and rapid swelling. The knee then gives way on turning. Young athletes, especially women, are most affected. Whether to reconstruct the ligament depends on the person's activity and instability. MedlinePlus describes the early picture: a popping sound or sensation at the moment of injury, obvious knee swelling within hours, pain that is worst when trying to put weight on the leg, an inability to carry on with the sport, and a feeling that the knee is unstable. Milder sprains may show up mainly as the knee giving way during use. Because the ligament is torn by a twisting load, the same force frequently damages the menisci, the joint cartilage or the collateral ligaments at the same time, which is why imaging looks beyond the ACL itself.
causes: Non-contact pivoting, cutting or landing injuries (70%)
Direct blows to the knee
riskFactors: Poor landing mechanics and hip weakness
signs: A pop at injury, swelling within hours (haemarthrosis)
Positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests
Giving way on pivoting
Positive pivot-shift test (rotational instability)
complications: Meniscal and cartilage damage
Recurrent instability
Early osteoarthritis
acl-injury.diagnosis: History and examination are frequently enough to make the diagnosis: the twisting mechanism, the pop, the rapid haemarthrosis and a positive Lachman, anterior drawer or pivot-shift test. Plain X-rays cannot show ligaments but are taken to rule out a fracture. MRI is the reference investigation: it confirms the rupture and shows the meniscal, cartilage, collateral ligament and bone injuries that commonly accompany it and that change the treatment plan.
acl-injury.treatment: Immediate: rest, ice, compression, elevation and early physiotherapy. Structured rehabilitation restores function in many people; surgical reconstruction with a tendon graft (hamstring, patellar or quadriceps) is chosen for those with instability or pivoting sports, followed by 9 to 12 months of rehabilitation. NHS Scotland musculoskeletal guidance describes three broad pathways: rehabilitation as the first-line treatment, with reconstruction reserved for people who develop functional instability; reconstruction followed by post-operative rehabilitation as the first choice; or a period of pre-operative rehabilitation and then reconstruction. The choice depends on the person's age and sporting demands, the severity of the damage and the expected long-term outcome. The evidence comparing the routes is mixed: a review found only low-quality data, showing no clear difference in patient-reported knee function between surgical reconstruction and rehabilitation alone. Orthopaedic referral is advised where there is persistent subjective instability, recurrent giving way, ongoing mechanical symptoms such as locking, or failure to regain near-symmetrical strength and hop-test performance.
acl-injury.prevention: Neuromuscular training programmes (landing technique, hip and hamstring strength, balance) cut injury rates by half in athletes.
acl-injury.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a knee that swelled rapidly after a twisting injury, cannot straighten, locks or feels unstable. People are advised to avoid sport until the knee has been clinically assessed.

disc-herniation.name: Herniated (slipped) disc
disc-herniation.definition: Protrusion of the soft nucleus of an intervertebral disc through its fibrous outer ring, most often at the lower lumbar levels, which can press on a nerve root.
disc-herniation.overview: Discs weaken with age and can bulge or rupture under load. Most herniations cause back pain alone; when the extruded material compresses a nerve root the result is sciatica: sharp pain, tingling and numbness shooting down the leg in that root's territory, sometimes with weakness. Nine in ten settle within three months without surgery. The lower back is by far the commonest site, followed by the neck; herniations in the upper and mid back are rare. Injury or strain can push the disc out of place or break it open. Without pressure on a nerve the result may be a low backache or no pain at all; with nerve pressure, pain, numbness or weakness follow the path of the affected nerve, typically down one side. Sciatica is the name for this pattern of leg symptoms, not a diagnosis in itself: a herniated disc is its leading cause, but spinal stenosis, piriformis syndrome, pelvic injury or fracture, tumours and spondylolisthesis can produce the same picture.
causes: Age-related disc degeneration
Lifting, twisting or a sudden strain
Repetitive loading
signs: Pain reproduced by straight-leg raising
Reduced ankle or knee reflex
Weak ankle dorsiflexion or big toe extension
Sensory loss in a dermatome
Pain, numbness or weakness following a single nerve's path down one leg
complications: Cauda equina syndrome (emergency)
Persistent nerve damage
Chronic pain
disc-herniation.diagnosis: Clinical, with MRI reserved for red flags, progressive neurological deficit or when surgery or injection is being considered, because disc bulges are common in people without symptoms. A plain spine X-ray cannot show the disc or confirm a herniation; MRI shows the disc, the nerve root and the degree of compression. Because other conditions, including nerve tumours, can mimic sciatica, imaging that does not match the clinical signs prompts a search for a non-disc cause.
disc-herniation.treatment: Stay active, pain relief (NSAIDs, short courses of stronger analgesia), physiotherapy, and time. Epidural steroid injections for severe radicular pain. Microdiscectomy for persistent sciatica beyond six to twelve weeks or for progressive weakness; emergency decompression for cauda equina syndrome. The first step is to stay active within comfort, with simple pain relief, followed by physiotherapy if symptoms persist; most people treated this way recover and return to normal activity. Anti-inflammatory medicines are used for mild to moderate pain, muscle relaxants for spasm, and short courses of stronger analgesia only when pain is severe and not responding. An epidural steroid injection is given under X-ray guidance so that the medicine reaches the exact level of the herniation. Surgery is considered when conservative treatment has not reduced the pain or when weakness progresses; only a minority of people with a symptomatic herniation need it.
disc-herniation.prevention: Lift with the legs, keep the back and core strong, healthy weight, do not smoke.
disc-herniation.seekCare: Emergency care for numbness around the saddle area, difficulty passing urine or controlling bowels, or weakness in both legs; urgent review for progressive weakness or unbearable pain.

gout.name: Gout
gout.definition: An inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of uric acid crystals in joints, triggered when blood urate is persistently high.
gout.overview: Uric acid is a waste product of purine metabolism. When its level exceeds saturation it crystallises in cool joints, classically the big toe, and the crystals provoke a sudden, exquisitely painful attack. Repeated attacks damage joints and form lumps (tophi). Lowering urate with medication dissolves the crystals and prevents attacks. Urate crystals can sit in a joint for a long time without causing symptoms; a flare is set off when something disturbs them, such as an infection, a joint injury, surgery, heavy drinking or certain foods. Flares typically bring intense pain, swelling and redness in one or more joints, last a week or two and then settle, and favour the joints furthest from the trunk: the toes, ankles, knees and fingers. Gout is several times commoner in men than in women. With early diagnosis, treatment and lifestyle changes, NIAMS describes it as one of the most controllable forms of arthritis.
causes: Reduced kidney excretion of urate (90%)
Overproduction: high purine diet, cell breakdown, rare enzyme defects
riskFactors: Alcohol (beer and spirits), sugary drinks, red meat and shellfish
Acute illness, surgery or joint injury as triggers
signs: A red, hot, shiny, extremely tender joint, often the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Tophi on the ears, fingers and elbows in chronic gout
A flare that settles over a week or two, leaving a normal-looking joint between attacks
complications: Joint damage and tophi
Kidney stones
Association with heart disease and kidney disease
gout.diagnosis: Crystals seen in joint fluid confirm it; a raised serum urate supports it (but may be normal during an attack); ultrasound or dual-energy CT shows crystal deposits. Infection must be excluded in a single hot joint. Gout is often diagnosed clinically from the history and examination. Aspirating fluid from the joint or bursa is the gold standard: the fluid is examined for urate crystals and tested for infection to exclude septic arthritis. Serum urate has limits: some people with gout have normal levels and many with high levels never develop gout, so clinicians may wait some weeks after a flare before measuring it.
gout.treatment: Attacks: NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids, started early; rest and ice. Prevention: allopurinol (or febuxostat) started after the attack settles and titrated to a target urate, with cover against flares for the first months; weight loss and diet changes. Treatment has two aims: easing the flare and preventing future flares and joint damage. Flares are treated with an NSAID such as ibuprofen, colchicine, or oral or injected corticosteroids, with paracetamol for additional pain relief. Where a medicine that raises urate is contributing, the prescriber may change it. Urate-lowering therapy is continued long term, because dissolving the crystals is what prevents further attacks and tophi; lifestyle changes such as losing weight, limiting alcohol and avoiding purine-rich foods support it.
gout.prevention: Healthy weight, limit alcohol and sugary drinks, moderate red meat and seafood, stay hydrated, review diuretics.
gout.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a hot swollen joint with fever, since septic arthritis looks identical and is an emergency. Joint fluid is tested for infection as well as crystals because septic arthritis can mimic gout.

sections.heading: What does a gout flare feel like?
sections.body:
Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in and around joints, and it causes sudden flares of severe pain and swelling. The big toe is the most common site, and the ankles, knees, hands and fingers can also be affected. Left untreated, an attack usually lasts about one to two weeks. If gout is not treated, future attacks may last even longer.

Further flares are common. StatPearls reports that around six in ten people have a second attack within a year, and the NHS notes that flares can come back every few months or after years. Without treatment, attacks tend to come more often and can affect more joints. Hard lumps of urate called tophi can also form under the skin, usually around the ears, fingers and elbows.

sections.heading: How is gout diagnosed?
sections.body:
A blood test for uric acid may be done, but the level in the blood often falls during a flare. Because of this, the test may be repeated some weeks after the flare has settled. A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out, and a raised urate level on its own, without joint symptoms, is not a diagnosis of gout.

When the diagnosis is uncertain, fluid can be taken from the joint and looked at under a microscope for crystals, which is regarded as the reference standard. The fluid can also be tested for infection, because gout and septic arthritis can occur together. An ultrasound or a special CT scan can also check for crystal build-up in the joint if fluid cannot be taken or the diagnosis is still unclear.

sections.heading: How is a gout flare treated?
sections.body:
Treatment has two parts: easing a flare, and preventing future flares. NICE recommends an NSAID (an anti-inflammatory painkiller), colchicine or a short course of steroid tablets as first-line treatment for a flare, depending on the person's other conditions, medicines and preferences. NICE found no strong evidence that any one of these works better than the others when used first.

A steroid injection into the joint or a muscle is considered if NSAIDs and colchicine cannot be used, are not tolerated or do not work. NIAMS notes that colchicine works best when started as soon as symptoms appear. NHS medicines information says it can take a day or two before pain and inflammation start to get better with colchicine. Ice packs can also ease symptoms, according to NHS inform.

sections.heading: How are future flares prevented?
sections.body:
NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment, which aims to clear the urate crystals and prevent flares. NICE says this treatment can also shrink tophi. NIAMS says a main goal of treatment is to prevent and resolve tophi so that joint damage stops.

Flares can increase when urate-lowering medicine is first started, so doctors may give another medicine alongside it for the first months. NICE recommends starting allopurinol low and increasing it slowly according to blood urate measurements. NIAMS says lifestyle changes alone are not enough when flares are frequent or tophi are present, so medicine is the main approach. The NHS says lifestyle changes can still help reduce future flares.

sections.heading: What diet and lifestyle changes help?
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It says beer is particularly bad because it contains a lot of purines, and that small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk. It advises losing weight gradually, and says extreme weight loss or starvation diets are not recommended because they can raise urate levels. The NHS also advises avoiding crash diets and lists dehydration as a possible trigger of an attack.

An NHS dietetic leaflet says regularly drinking sugar-sweetened drinks can increase the risk of gout, while sugar-free fizzy drinks do not. Versus Arthritis lists a daily glass of skimmed milk among its management tips. NHS inform notes that vitamin C supplements are not suitable for everyone and recommends talking to a GP before using them.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
Leaving gout untreated may cause lasting damage to the joints, and the NHS notes that repeated attacks can damage joints and cause kidney stones. Severe gout pain can lead to feelings of depression or anxiety, according to NHS inform.

The NHS advises a GP appointment for a first episode of gout symptoms, or when usual treatments are not helping. For a painful swollen joint that is getting worse, especially with a very high temperature, feeling hot or shivery, or feeling sick or unable to eat, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis. Gout can look the same as septic arthritis, which is why fluid from the joint may be tested for infection.

faqs.q: How long does a gout attack last?
faqs.a: Left untreated, a gout attack usually lasts about one to two weeks, and later attacks may last even longer. The NHS notes that flares can come back every few months or after years. NHS medicines information says colchicine can take a day or two before pain and inflammation start to get better.

faqs.q: Does gout go away on its own?
faqs.a: Without treatment, a flare usually lasts about one to two weeks, according to the NHS, but further flares are common. StatPearls reports that around six in ten people have a second attack within a year. NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment to prevent flares. The NHS advises seeing a GP when usual treatments are not helping.

faqs.q: Should I have a uric acid blood test during a flare?
faqs.a: The level of urate in the blood often falls during a flare, so a test then can be misleading. The test may be repeated some weeks after the flare has settled. A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out, and a raised level on its own, without joint symptoms, is not a diagnosis of gout.

faqs.q: Is beer worse than wine for gout?
faqs.a: Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks. It says beer is particularly bad because it contains a lot of purines, while small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk. An Oxford Kidney Unit leaflet advises people prone to gout attacks to reduce alcohol to a minimum or avoid it.

faqs.q: When should I get urgent help for a swollen joint?
faqs.a: For a painful swollen joint that is getting worse, especially with a very high temperature or feeling sick or unable to eat, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111. These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis. The NHS advises a GP appointment for a first episode of gout symptoms.

type-1-diabetes.name: Type 1 diabetes
type-1-diabetes.definition: An autoimmune disease in which the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas are destroyed, so the body cannot regulate blood glucose without injected insulin.
type-1-diabetes.overview: Type 1 diabetes usually appears in childhood or young adulthood over days to weeks: thirst, frequent urination, weight loss and tiredness as glucose spills into the urine. Without insulin the body burns fat uncontrollably and produces acid (ketoacidosis), which is fatal untreated. Lifelong insulin replacement, increasingly with pumps and continuous glucose monitors, allows a full life. The NHS lists passing urine more than usual, especially at night, intense thirst, marked tiredness and unintended weight loss as the classic early signs, with blurred vision, fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and recurrent infections also possible; symptoms develop over a few days or weeks. Thirst and dehydration arise because the kidneys draw water from the body to clear excess glucose into the urine. Diabetic ketoacidosis is sometimes the first sign in someone not yet diagnosed: without insulin, ketones accumulate and make the blood acidic, and infection, injury, serious illness, missed insulin doses or the stress of surgery can tip someone with known diabetes into it.
causes: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells in genetically susceptible people, possibly triggered by viral infection
signs: Weight loss, dehydration
Ketone smell, deep sighing breathing and drowsiness in ketoacidosis
Blurred vision, slow-healing cuts and recurrent infections
Fruity-smelling breath
complications: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hypoglycaemia from insulin
Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy
Cardiovascular disease
Foot ulcers
Ketoacidosis triggered by infection, injury, serious illness, missed insulin or surgery
type-1-diabetes.diagnosis: Raised blood glucose with symptoms; ketones in blood or urine; antibodies (GAD, IA-2) and low C-peptide confirm type 1. HbA1c tracks control over months. Where a raised glucose is found in someone without symptoms, testing is repeated on a later day to confirm it. Autoantibody testing helps distinguish type 1 from other forms of diabetes, which is harder in children who are also obese.
type-1-diabetes.treatment: Insulin from diagnosis, as multiple daily injections (long-acting plus rapid-acting with meals) or a pump, matched to carbohydrate intake; glucose monitoring; structured education; annual screening of eyes, kidneys and feet; blood pressure and cholesterol control. Ketoacidosis is treated in hospital with insulin and fluids, and the underlying trigger, such as an infection, is treated at the same time. Early hypoglycaemia causes anxiety, sweating, hunger, tremor, palpitations and pallor; untreated it can progress to confusion, behavioural change, loss of consciousness, seizures and coma, which is why people on insulin and those around them are taught to recognise and treat it promptly.
type-1-diabetes.prevention: None yet, although immunotherapy can delay onset in high-risk relatives; good control lowers the risk of complications.
type-1-diabetes.seekCare: See a GP urgently, the same day for a child or young person, for increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss: these can be the first signs of type 1 diabetes. Emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion in someone with diabetes, or for severe hypoglycaemia (confusion, seizure, unconsciousness). NHS advice is to call 999 or go to A&E if symptoms worsen quickly, or if the person becomes sleepy or confused or starts breathing faster and deeper than usual.

sections.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
sections.body:
Type 1 diabetes is a lifelong condition in which the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is an autoimmune condition: the immune system damages the insulin-producing cells of the pancreas.

Type 1 diabetes can run in families, but Diabetes UK says most people with type 1 have no family history of it. Diabetes UK says the exact cause of type 1 diabetes is not known, and that things in the environment, such as viruses, may play a part in triggering it.

In the UK, Diabetes UK reports that about 90% of people diagnosed with diabetes have type 2 and about 8% have type 1. The NHS lists the classic early signs as needing the toilet more, being thirsty, feeling tired and losing weight, often remembered as the four Ts. NIDDK notes that some people first find out they have type 1 diabetes when they develop signs of diabetic ketoacidosis.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP will usually test a urine sample and may check blood glucose, then send the person to hospital for assessment. The NHS says people are usually kept in hospital until their blood test results are back.

NIDDK says symptoms of type 1 diabetes usually develop quickly, over a few days or weeks. The other signs it lists are blurred vision, sweet or fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections.

Because diabetic ketoacidosis can be the first sign, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms worsen quickly, or if stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing develop. The NHS advises seeing a GP about these symptoms, and calling 999 or going to A&E if they get worse quickly.

sections.heading: How is type 1 diabetes treated day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says people with type 1 diabetes take insulin, either with pens or with a pump. Most people take both a long-acting insulin and a rapid-acting insulin before meals. This pattern is known as basal-bolus treatment.

Insulin can be given with pens or by a pump, which gives small amounts of rapid-acting insulin throughout the day. Pump therapy can be used by adults, teenagers and children with adult supervision.

The NHS says the dose of rapid-acting insulin at a meal is worked out from the amount of carbohydrate to be eaten, which is called carbohydrate counting.

One NHS 111 Wales page stresses that treatment should not be stopped during illness, and that the treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed.

sections.heading: What is a hypo?
sections.body:
A hypo is a lower-than-normal level of glucose in the blood. The NHS lists feeling hungry, dizzy, sweaty and shaky among the signs of a hypo, and says that if it is not treated it can lead to drowsiness or loss of consciousness.

 Common triggers include too much insulin, a skipped meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

Mild hypos are usually treated with something sugary. In a severe hypo a person may become drowsy, confused or lose consciousness and may need a glucagon injection into a muscle or glucose given into a vein; the NHS says to call 999 and ask for an ambulance if they do not come round within 10 minutes of a glucagon injection.

NICE says the annual review should check that the person can recognise the symptoms of a hypo.

sections.heading: What is diabetic ketoacidosis?
sections.body:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a medical emergency that can follow untreated type 1 diabetes and is treated in hospital with insulin and fluids. Diabetes UK lists being very thirsty, needing to wee more often, feeling tired and sleepy, confusion, blurred vision, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, and sweet or fruity-smelling breath; the NHS also lists breathing more deeply than usual. Diabetes UK and the NHS say DKA symptoms usually develop over about 24 hours but can come on faster.

The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if ketone levels are high, or if there are symptoms of DKA and the ketone level is not known.

NHS inform says untreated DKA can lead to unconsciousness, so the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the warning signs appear.

sections.heading: What are the long-term complications and checks?
sections.body:
Over time, high glucose can damage blood vessels and nerves. The NHS describes complications affecting the eyes, feet and kidneys. In the eyes, damage to blood vessels can cause sight problems (diabetic retinopathy) and, uncommonly, blindness, so adults and children aged 12 or over are offered eye screening every year. In the feet, nerve damage means small cuts may go unnoticed and can become ulcers, so the NHS advises checking the feet every day and having a foot examination at least once a year. In the kidneys, damage usually causes no symptoms at first, so a test is advised every year.

NICE says the annual review for adults includes foot checks and checks for complications such as kidney and nerve problems, and advice about the higher risk of gum disease. NICE says children with type 1 diabetes should have their blood pressure checked every year after they turn 12.

faqs.q: Is type 1 diabetes the same as type 2?
faqs.a: No. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition in which the body makes little or no insulin. Type 2 is a different condition; in the UK about 90% of people diagnosed with diabetes have type 2, according to Diabetes UK.

faqs.q: What are the four Ts of type 1 diabetes?
faqs.a: The NHS lists needing the toilet more, thirst, tiredness and weight loss as the core signs, often remembered as the four Ts. Blurred vision, fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and frequent infections can also occur.

faqs.q: Why do hypos happen?
faqs.a: Common triggers include taking too much insulin, skipping a meal, vigorous exercise and drinking alcohol on an empty stomach.

faqs.q: Should insulin carry on during illness?
faqs.a: One NHS 111 Wales page says it is very important not to stop treatment when ill. The treatment plan may say whether a temporary increase is needed, and the diabetes care team is the place to ask.

faqs.q: When is diabetic ketoacidosis an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if symptoms are getting worse quickly, or if there is stomach pain, sleepiness or confusion, or fast, deep breathing. DKA is a medical emergency that is treated in hospital.

type-2-diabetes.name: Type 2 diabetes
type-2-diabetes.definition: A metabolic disease in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance) and the pancreas gradually fails to compensate, leaving blood glucose persistently high.
type-2-diabetes.overview: Type 2 diabetes accounts for over 90% of diabetes and is closely tied to excess weight and inactivity, though genes matter greatly. It develops silently over years; many people are diagnosed on a routine test or when a complication appears. Sustained weight loss early on can put it into remission.
causes: Insulin resistance from visceral fat and inactivity, plus progressive beta-cell failure, on a strong genetic background
riskFactors: Age over 40 (younger in South Asian, Black and Hispanic populations)
signs: Often none
Central obesity, acanthosis nigricans
Reduced foot sensation and pulses in established disease
Retinal changes
complications: Heart attack and stroke
Kidney failure
Retinopathy and blindness
Neuropathy, foot ulcers and amputation
Fatty liver disease
Hyperosmolar crisis
type-2-diabetes.diagnosis: HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more, or fasting glucose of 7 mmol/L or more, repeated if without symptoms. Annual checks of kidney function, urine albumin, eyes, feet, blood pressure and lipids.
type-2-diabetes.treatment: Diet, weight loss and activity are the foundation; metformin first, then SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas or insulin as needed; statins and blood pressure treatment reduce cardiovascular risk; structured education and foot care.
type-2-diabetes.prevention: Diet and exercise programmes halve the risk in people with prediabetes; keeping a healthy weight and staying active are the key measures.
type-2-diabetes.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, or for drowsiness or confusion with very high glucose readings. Get same-day advice from a GP or NHS 111 for a foot wound that is red, hot or discharging, or sudden vision change.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of type 2 diabetes and how does it develop?
sections.body:
Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at first, and signs can build slowly over a few years. The NHS lists tiredness, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss as the most common symptoms. Other possible signs are blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, and genital itching or repeated thrush. NHS inform also lists tingling or numbness, which can point to nerve damage.

NHS 111 Wales describes type 2 diabetes as often associated with being overweight or inactive, or with a family history of the condition. The NHS explains that in type 2 diabetes the body either does not make enough insulin or the insulin it makes does not work correctly. NHS 111 Wales advises speaking to a GP about any of these symptoms or about worries over personal risk.

sections.heading: How is type 2 diabetes diagnosed, and what do check-ups involve?
sections.body:
A GP can usually diagnose type 2 diabetes with a blood test and a urine test. NHS Scotland guidance describes HbA1c as the preferred diagnostic test, because it does not require fasting and reflects average blood glucose over the previous few months.

After diagnosis, NICE describes a yearly check-up called the annual review. NICE says it includes checking blood pressure, blood glucose and cardiovascular risk, with regular foot checks, and covers other long-term complications such as kidney and nerve problems. Diabetes UK and NHS material on annual checks also list a urine test for kidney protein and a retinal eye screen. Eye screening is a photograph of the back of the eye, and it is not the same as a routine optician sight test.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for type 2 diabetes?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment usually combines lifestyle changes with medicines. Its treatment page centres on diet, physical activity, weight and smoking, and suggests eating more wholegrains, pulses, fruit and vegetables.

For people without other serious conditions, the NHS describes the usual starting point as metformin together with an SGLT2 inhibitor, which lowers blood sugar by letting extra sugar leave the body in urine. If metformin causes side effects, an SGLT2 inhibitor alone may be recommended. A GLP-1 agonist, given by injection, may be offered to people with a history of heart disease or with obesity when other treatments have not lowered blood sugar enough. Local NHS guidance also describes gliclazide, sitagliptin and pioglitazone as further options.

sections.heading: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission, and when is insulin needed?
sections.body:
Diabetes UK says type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission, mainly through weight loss. It avoids the word cure because there is no evidence that remission could remain permanent, and many people who regain weight come out of remission.

The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using products such as soups and shakes, to eligible people in England who have type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity. NHS England notes that the strict nature of the diet means it is not suitable for everyone. The NHS also advises against very strict low-calorie diets without medical advice, especially for people taking insulin or other diabetes medicines.

The NHS says insulin is prescribed for type 2 diabetes if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range.

sections.heading: What complications can type 2 diabetes cause, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
Over time, high blood sugar can damage the blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums. The NHS lists coronary heart disease and stroke, foot problems where untreated ulcers or infections can lead to amputation, sight problems such as diabetic retinopathy, kidney problems and gum disease. It also says that controlling blood sugar and having regular check-ups is the best way to lower the risk of complications.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and HHS are rare in type 2 diabetes but can be life threatening. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if someone with type 2 diabetes is peeing a lot, feels very thirsty, feels sick, is confused or very sleepy, or is short of breath. NHS inform advises contacting a podiatrist or GP practice urgently for a hot, red, swollen foot or new skin damage, and phoning NHS 111 if the practice is closed.

sections.heading: Living with type 2 diabetes: eating, activity and daily checks
sections.body:
The NHS suggests a healthy diet that includes fruit, vegetables, wholegrain foods such as wholemeal bread and oats, and pulses such as chickpeas and lentils. It also notes that having diabetes increases the harmful effects of smoking.

NICE recommends structured education for adults with type 2 diabetes at the time of diagnosis, with yearly reinforcement and review. Diabetes UK says people should be offered a free diabetes education course. NICE says the care team can point people to support groups, and people can ask for help or advice at any time.

NHS Lanarkshire advises checking the feet every day for cuts, skin breaks or hard skin. NHS 111 Wales says people who take insulin for type 2 diabetes must tell the DVLA, because of the risk of low blood sugar.

faqs.q: Can type 2 diabetes go into remission?
faqs.a: Diabetes UK says type 2 diabetes can sometimes go into remission, mainly through weight loss, though it is not guaranteed to last. The NHS England Path to Remission Programme offers a low-calorie total diet replacement plan, using soups and shakes, to eligible people in England with type 2 diabetes and overweight or obesity.

faqs.q: How is type 2 diabetes different from type 1?
faqs.a: The NHS says that in type 2 diabetes the body either does not make enough insulin or the insulin it makes does not work correctly. MedlinePlus describes type 1 as an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing cells, so little or no insulin is made.

faqs.q: Does everyone with type 2 diabetes need insulin?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment usually combines lifestyle changes with medicines, and that insulin is prescribed if other diabetes medicines no longer keep blood glucose within a healthy range. NHS 111 Wales notes that insulin is not often used in the early years.

faqs.q: Can someone have type 2 diabetes without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says symptoms may come on gradually and not everyone gets them, and NHS inform notes that signs often appear slowly over a few years, so some people do not realise they have it. NHS 111 Wales advises speaking to a GP about any symptoms or worries over risk.

faqs.q: When is type 2 diabetes an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if someone with type 2 diabetes is peeing a lot, feels very thirsty, feels sick, is confused or very sleepy, or is short of breath, as these can signal DKA or HHS. The NHS says both are rare in type 2 diabetes but can be life threatening.

keyFacts.label: Usual starting medicines
keyFacts.value: The NHS describes metformin with an SGLT2 inhibitor as the usual starting point for people without other serious conditions.

keyFacts.label: Common symptoms
keyFacts.value: Tiredness, needing to pee more, constant thirst and unintended weight loss; many people have none at first.

keyFacts.label: How it is found
keyFacts.value: A GP can usually diagnose it with blood and urine tests.

keyFacts.label: Yearly check-up
keyFacts.value: NICE describes an annual review covering blood pressure, blood glucose, cardiovascular risk and foot checks.

keyFacts.label: Long-term risks
keyFacts.value: Damage to blood vessels, nerves, eyes, kidneys, feet and gums.

keyFacts.label: Remission
keyFacts.value: Possible for some people; NHS England runs a Path to Remission Programme for eligible people.

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 or go to A&E if peeing a lot, very thirsty, feeling sick, confused, very sleepy or short of breath.

hypothyroidism.name: Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
hypothyroidism.definition: Insufficient thyroid hormone, most often because the immune system destroys the thyroid gland, slowing the body's metabolism.
hypothyroidism.overview: Thyroxine sets the pace of nearly every cell, so its lack slows everything: energy, thought, bowel, heart rate and heat production. Symptoms creep in over months and are easily mistaken for ageing or depression. A simple blood test makes the diagnosis and a daily tablet of levothyroxine restores normal life. Symptoms are non-specific and gradual: difficulty concentrating, low mood, hair loss, a hoarse voice and heavier or irregular periods are common additions to tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and dry skin. No single symptom reliably identifies the condition, and many people with mild (subclinical) hypothyroidism have no symptoms at all, so attributing a given complaint to the thyroid can be difficult. Hashimoto's disease, in which the immune system attacks the thyroid, is the most common cause where iodine intake is adequate; iodine deficiency remains the commonest cause worldwide.

Treatment of an overactive thyroid (radioiodine, surgery)
Iodine deficiency worldwide
Drugs: amiodarone, lithium, immunotherapy
Pituitary failure (rare)
Congenital
Thyroiditis (inflammation of the gland)
Radiotherapy to the neck
signs: Weight gain, dry skin and hair, puffy face
Slow pulse, cold intolerance
Slow-relaxing reflexes
Goitre
Hoarse voice, constipation, heavy periods
Enlarged thyroid felt on examination of the neck
Muscle weakness, aches and cramps
complications: High cholesterol and heart disease
Depression and cognitive slowing
Infertility and pregnancy complications
Myxoedema coma (rare, life-threatening)
Premature birth and other pregnancy complications when untreated
hypothyroidism.diagnosis: A raised TSH with a low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism; thyroid peroxidase antibodies indicate the autoimmune cause. Cholesterol is often raised. A GP typically asks about symptoms, examines the neck for an enlarged thyroid and arranges blood tests. Because hypothyroidism contributes to high cholesterol, people found to have raised cholesterol are tested for it.
hypothyroidism.treatment: Levothyroxine once daily on an empty stomach, dose adjusted by TSH every six to eight weeks until stable, then checked yearly; higher doses are needed in pregnancy. Dosing starts low and rises gradually, with regular blood tests until the right dose is found; some people feel better within weeks, others take months, and treatment is usually lifelong. Side effects such as sweating, chest pain, headaches and sleep problems mostly occur when the dose is too high. Extra care is needed in people with heart conditions, diabetes or adrenal problems. People who are mildly affected with few or no symptoms may not need treatment and are simply monitored. An unusually high dose requirement prompts a check for absorption problems, missed doses or coeliac disease.
hypothyroidism.prevention: Adequate iodine intake; screening in pregnancy and after thyroid treatment. Pregnant women taking levothyroxine usually need more frequent testing, and the dose often changes.
hypothyroidism.seekCare: See a doctor for persistent tiredness with weight gain, cold intolerance or low mood; emergency care for drowsiness, very low temperature or confusion in someone with known hypothyroidism. Myxoedema coma, an extreme form in which the body's functions slow to a life-threatening point, needs immediate hospital treatment.

sections.heading: What does an underactive thyroid feel like?
sections.body:
An underactive thyroid develops slowly, and symptoms may not show for months or even years. Because the changes build up gradually, some people go months or even years without noticing symptoms. The NHS lists common symptoms such as feeling very tired, putting on weight, feeling colder than usual and constipation. A croaky or hoarse voice is also described, and some women have heavy or irregular periods. Symptoms often resemble those of other conditions, which can delay recognition.

Many of these problems have other explanations, so a blood test that measures hormone levels is the only accurate way to confirm a thyroid problem. The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as usually lifelong, and says it can be managed with medicine.

sections.heading: What causes an underactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The main cause in the UK is Hashimoto's disease, which is an autoimmune condition. Autoimmune means the body's defence system mistakenly attacks its own tissue, in this case the thyroid. Inflammation of the thyroid, called thyroiditis, is another cause. Not getting enough iodine in the diet can also be a cause, but the NHS says this is rare in the UK.

Surgery or radiotherapy around the neck or thyroid can also lead to it. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to it as well. The NIDDK says people who receive radioactive iodine treatment will probably eventually develop an underactive thyroid. Certain medicines, including lithium, amiodarone and interferon alpha, have been linked to the condition. Some babies are born with an underactive thyroid, which is called congenital hypothyroidism.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP may ask about symptoms and may feel the neck to check whether the thyroid is enlarged. The TSH blood test needs no special preparation, according to MedlinePlus. MedlinePlus also says biotin (vitamin B7) can distort TSH results. TSH is a hormone made by the pituitary gland that tells the thyroid how much to produce. A high level of TSH together with a low level of thyroid hormone (T4) can point to an underactive thyroid.

When Hashimoto's disease is suspected, a blood test for thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies can be used, and the NIDDK says it is positive in most people with the condition. An ultrasound scan may be used if antibodies are not found but Hashimoto's disease is still suspected. The NIDDK says ultrasound can also help rule out other causes of an enlarged thyroid, such as nodules. The NIDDK adds that further testing is usually unnecessary to confirm the diagnosis.

sections.heading: How is an underactive thyroid treated?
sections.body:
The usual treatment is levothyroxine tablets. Levothyroxine replaces the thyroid hormone the body is missing. NHS inform says people usually need to take it for the rest of their lives. Some people with very mild symptoms, or none, may not need any treatment.

Regular blood tests are used at the start until the right dose is found. A follow-up blood test is usually arranged after a dose is started or changed. The NIDDK says the condition can most likely be controlled with thyroid hormone medicine as long as the recommended dose is taken as instructed. The NIDDK also warns that taking too much thyroid hormone medicine can cause serious problems, such as atrial fibrillation (an irregular heart rhythm) or osteoporosis (weak bones). NHS guidance says the wrong dose can cause side effects such as feeling sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, babies and children
sections.body:
The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or trying to conceive with an underactive thyroid. Further tests are needed, and the levothyroxine dose will probably change during pregnancy. Untreated, an underactive thyroid in pregnancy can raise the chance of problems such as pre-eclampsia, birth defects, premature birth or miscarriage.

Congenital hypothyroidism, an underactive thyroid present from birth, often has subtle signs or none at birth. This is why newborn screening matters. A clinical review reports that growth and development return to normal with early and adequate treatment. Some babies have a temporary form of the condition. Another review says some children treated early still have mild hearing deficits, so hearing should be checked periodically.

sections.heading: What are the complications and the outlook?
sections.body:
NHS 111 Wales says an underactive thyroid is not usually serious if the right treatment is being given. Untreated, it raises the risk of cardiovascular disease, according to the NHS, and NHS 111 Wales lists bone problems including osteoporosis. The NHS also lists goitre, which is an enlarged thyroid gland, and problems in pregnancy as possible complications.

A cardiology review describes the heart effects as typically reversible with hormone replacement. Myxoedema coma is a very rare but life-threatening complication that needs emergency hospital treatment. The route to care for myxoedema coma is to call 999. The NHS says treatment usually involves thyroid hormone replacement medicine given directly into a vein.

faqs.q: Is an underactive thyroid permanent?
faqs.a: NHS inform says people usually need to take levothyroxine for the rest of their lives. Regular blood tests are used at the start to find the right dose. Some people with very mild or no symptoms may not need treatment. The NIDDK says it can most likely be controlled with thyroid hormone medicine taken as instructed.

faqs.q: What is Hashimoto's disease?
faqs.a: Hashimoto's disease is an autoimmune condition in which the body's defence system attacks the thyroid. It is the main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK, according to the NHS. The NHS says it is most common in women and usually starts between the ages of 30 and 50. A blood test for TPO antibodies can be part of the check, and the NIDDK says it is positive in most people with the condition.

faqs.q: How do doctors confirm an underactive thyroid?
faqs.a: A GP may ask about symptoms and may feel the neck to check whether the thyroid is enlarged. A blood test measuring hormone levels is the only accurate way to confirm a thyroid problem. A high TSH with a low T4 can point to an underactive thyroid.

faqs.q: Can an underactive thyroid affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: Untreated, it can raise the chance of problems such as pre-eclampsia, premature birth or miscarriage. The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or trying to conceive. Extra tests are then needed, and the levothyroxine dose will probably change during pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can an underactive thyroid be dangerous?
faqs.a: It is not usually serious with the right treatment, according to the NHS. Untreated, it can raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and of bone problems such as osteoporosis. Myxoedema coma is very rare but life-threatening and needs emergency hospital treatment, and the route to care is 999.

hyperthyroidism.name: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
hyperthyroidism.definition: Excess thyroid hormone, most often from Graves' disease, in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid to overproduce.
hyperthyroidism.overview: Too much thyroxine speeds the body up: weight loss despite appetite, tremor, palpitations, sweating, anxiety and diarrhoea. Graves' disease can also inflame the eye muscles, pushing the eyes forward. Treatment blocks hormone production, destroys thyroid tissue with radioiodine, or removes the gland. Thyroid hormones regulate how the body uses energy, so an excess touches nearly every organ, including the rhythm of the heart. Older adults may present differently, with loss of appetite or withdrawal from people rather than restlessness, and the condition is sometimes mistaken for depression or dementia. Thyroid eye disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy), with dryness, redness, protrusion or double vision, affects a minority of people whose overactive thyroid is due to Graves' disease. The course depends on the cause: thyroiditis may settle without treatment as stored hormone is used up, whereas Graves' disease usually worsens over time if left untreated.

Rarely, a non-cancerous pituitary tumour; iodine contrast dye mainly matters when the thyroid already has a problem

complications: Atrial fibrillation and heart failure
Osteoporosis

Thyroid storm (rare, life-threatening)

hyperthyroidism.diagnosis: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves'; a radioiodine uptake scan distinguishes causes when antibodies are negative. Assessment starts with the history and a blood test of thyroid function. If the blood test confirms overactivity, further tests identify the cause, because the cause determines treatment. The diagnosis is usually prompted by unexplained weight loss, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or persistent nervousness and tiredness.
hyperthyroidism.treatment: Beta blockers for symptoms; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil) for 12 to 18 months; radioiodine or thyroidectomy for relapse or large goitres, followed by levothyroxine replacement. Eye disease needs specialist care and stopping smoking. Antithyroid medicines reduce hormone production; radioactive iodine destroys thyroid cells; surgery removes part or all of the gland; and beta blockers such as propranolol ease a rapid heartbeat while definitive treatment takes effect. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid later, which then needs lifelong hormone replacement.
hyperthyroidism.prevention: Not smoking reduces eye disease; no prevention for the autoimmune process itself.
hyperthyroidism.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with breathlessness or chest pain, fever with confusion and agitation, or sudden vision change or eye pain. NHS and NIDDK advice is to see a GP for unexplained weight loss, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or persistent nervousness and tiredness, since untreated hyperthyroidism can cause serious heart problems.

sections.heading: What does an overactive thyroid feel like?
sections.body:
The symptoms of an overactive thyroid can appear gradually or suddenly, and they vary in how severe they are. People often notice nervousness, irritability, mood swings, poor sleep and persistent tiredness. Other changes include sensitivity to heat and a tremor. Some people also have swelling in the neck from an enlarged thyroid gland, called a goitre. Because many of these symptoms can have other causes, symptoms alone cannot confirm the diagnosis.

In older adults the picture can look different, with loss of appetite and apathy rather than restlessness. For this reason the condition can be mistaken for depression or dementia in older people. The NHS advises seeing a GP for symptoms or signs of an overactive thyroid. A blood test of thyroid function is the usual first step.

sections.heading: What causes an overactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The most common cause is Graves' disease, an autoimmune condition. The NHS says about 4 in every 5 people with an overactive thyroid have Graves' disease. Other causes include thyroid nodules and inflammation of the gland called thyroiditis. The NHS says too much iodine, for example from medicines that contain it such as amiodarone, can also trigger an overactive thyroid. The NHS describes thyroiditis as swelling of the thyroid, which can cause extra thyroid hormones to be produced. A recent iodine load, such as from amiodarone or contrast dye, can make an uptake scan unreliable, so an antibody test may be used instead.

Further tests can help to tell the causes apart. An antibody blood test can help identify Graves' disease. A radioactive iodine uptake scan can also help, with high uptake typical of Graves' disease and low uptake typical of thyroiditis.

sections.heading: How is an overactive thyroid diagnosed?
sections.body: The starting point is a visit to a GP, who may arrange a thyroid function blood test. A diagnosis is based on the symptoms and the results of blood tests that assess how well the thyroid is working. These tests measure thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and the thyroid hormones T3 and T4. A low TSH with a high T3 or T4 usually points to an overactive thyroid. A mild form with a low TSH but normal T3 and T4 is called subclinical hyperthyroidism. Thyroid UK says many cases settle by themselves, so regular TSH checks are needed. Thyroid UK also says an undetectable TSH carries a higher risk of progressing to overt hyperthyroidism. Other blood tests and a thyroid uptake scan may be used to find the cause.

sections.heading: What are the treatments for an overactive thyroid?
sections.body:
The NHS describes three main treatments: medicine, radioactive iodine treatment and surgery. Antithyroid medicines such as carbimazole and propylthiouracil are a common first choice. They are usually taken for more than a year, and the medicine is then stopped to see whether the condition returns. Some people need to continue the medicine for several years or possibly for life. Beta-blockers, such as propranolol or atenolol, can relieve symptoms such as tremor and a rapid heartbeat, but they are not suitable for people with asthma.

Radioactive iodine is a highly effective treatment, and often a single dose is enough. It is not suitable for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or for people with severe eye problems caused by the condition. Surgery is reserved for cases such as a large goitre, severe eye problems, when other treatments cannot be used, or when symptoms return. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid, which is sometimes temporary but often permanent and needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.

sections.heading: Can an overactive thyroid affect the eyes?
sections.body:
Eye problems, known as thyroid eye disease or Graves' ophthalmopathy, can occur in people whose overactive thyroid is caused by Graves' disease. NHS pages give different figures, from around 1 in 20 to around 1 in 4 people with Graves' disease. Symptoms can include dry and gritty eyes, red eyes, sensitivity to light, watering, blurred or double vision, and bulging eyes. Severe disease can cause vision loss, and treatments named by NHS inform include eye drops, sunglasses, corticosteroids, radiotherapy and surgery. Smoking increases the risk of thyroid eye disease, and quitting helps. Thyroid UK says eye problems can continue in people who keep smoking after their thyroid is treated.

An NHS hospital leaflet advises getting urgent advice from a doctor if the eyes become more prominent and swollen, for example from the GP the same day or NHS 111.

sections.heading: What about pregnancy?
sections.body: NIDDK says a woman with mild hyperthyroidism in pregnancy probably will not need treatment. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism in pregnancy can lead to serious problems for the mother and the baby, according to NIDDK. NIDDK says more severe cases are typically treated with antithyroid medicines, most often propylthiouracil early in pregnancy. Radioactive iodine is not suitable during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and NIDDK says it can damage the baby's thyroid gland. NHS inform says becoming pregnant can lead to a relapse of symptoms, especially in someone with a history of Graves' disease. A UK hospital trust guideline suggests ultrasound scans in later pregnancy to watch the baby's growth when the mother has hyperthyroidism. Antibodies from a mother with Graves' disease can cross the placenta and affect the baby's thyroid function, according to a systematic review.

sections.heading: What are the complications and outlook?
sections.body: An overactive thyroid is usually treatable, according to the NHS. The NHS says an overactive thyroid can raise the risk of atrial fibrillation, heart failure and osteoporosis, which weakens the bones. Atrial fibrillation is an irregular and often abnormally fast heart rhythm. Rarely, an undiagnosed or poorly controlled overactive thyroid can lead to thyroid storm, a serious, life-threatening condition. The NHS lists triggers such as infection, pregnancy, missed doses of medicine and physical damage to the thyroid. Warning signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness. Severe thyroid eye disease can lead to vision loss, and radioactive iodine can leave the thyroid underactive. Thyroid storm is an emergency, and anyone with these signs needs 999.

faqs.q: Can an overactive thyroid get better without treatment?
faqs.a: A mild form with a low TSH but normal hormone levels, called subclinical hyperthyroidism, is often monitored with regular TSH checks, and Thyroid UK says many cases settle by themselves. Other people are treated with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Some need medicine for several years or possibly for life. A GP can arrange the thyroid blood test that starts the process.

faqs.q: Is an overactive thyroid the same as an underactive thyroid?
faqs.a: No, an overactive thyroid makes too much thyroid hormone, while an underactive thyroid means hormone levels are too low. Radioactive iodine treatment for an overactive thyroid often leads to an underactive thyroid, which is sometimes temporary but often permanent. A permanent underactive thyroid needs long-term thyroid hormone medicine.

faqs.q: When is an overactive thyroid an emergency?
faqs.a: Thyroid storm is rare but life-threatening, and can occur when an overactive thyroid is undiagnosed or poorly controlled. Its signs include a rapid heartbeat, high temperature, confusion and loss of consciousness. Anyone with these signs needs an emergency response, so call 999.

faqs.q: Who cannot have radioactive iodine treatment?
faqs.a: NHS hospital guidance says radioactive iodine is not suitable in pregnancy or breastfeeding. It is also not suitable where eye disease is severe. Surgery is reserved for cases such as a large goitre, severe eye problems, when other treatments cannot be used, or when symptoms return.

faqs.q: Can an overactive thyroid be mistaken for something else?
faqs.a: Yes, many of its symptoms can have other causes, so symptoms alone cannot confirm it. In older adults it can be mistaken for depression or dementia. The symptoms can appear gradually or suddenly and vary in how severe they are. A thyroid function blood test helps to show whether a thyroid problem is responsible.

urinary-tract-infection.name: Urinary tract infection
urinary-tract-infection.definition: Bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis) or, when it ascends, the kidney (pyelonephritis), usually by gut bacteria such as Escherichia coli.
urinary-tract-infection.overview: UTIs are among the commonest bacterial infections, far more frequent in women because the short urethra lets bacteria reach the bladder easily. Cystitis burns and nags but is rarely dangerous; kidney infection causes fever, loin pain and vomiting and can lead to sepsis, especially in the elderly, in pregnancy and with obstruction. Infection begins when bacteria enter the urethra and move upwards to the bladder (cystitis) and sometimes on to the kidneys (pyelonephritis); E. coli is the main agent, and other bacteria, viruses or fungi are rare causes. Presentation varies with age: infants often have fever, irritability or poor feeding, while older adults may have no urinary symptoms and instead show confusion resembling dementia, marked fatigue or incontinence. UTI is the most common hospital-acquired infection, and most of those cases are associated with urinary catheters. Resistance to antibiotics is an increasing problem in treating UTI.
causes: Gut bacteria (E. coli in 80%) ascending the urethra
Catheters and instrumentation
Obstruction: stones, enlarged prostate
riskFactors: Female anatomy (a short urethra close to the vagina and anus), sexual activity, spermicides
Incomplete bladder emptying, kidney stones, prostate enlargement
signs: Suprapubic tenderness
Loin tenderness and fever in pyelonephritis
Confusion in older adults
Cloudy or bloody urine
In infants: fever, irritability and reduced feeding
In older adults: dementia-like confusion, fatigue or new incontinence without urinary complaints
complications: Kidney infection and abscess
Sepsis
Kidney scarring in children
Premature labour in pregnancy
Recurrent infection, defined as repeated episodes within a few months
Hospital-acquired, catheter-associated infection
urinary-tract-infection.diagnosis: Symptoms and a urine dipstick (nitrites, leucocytes, blood) in uncomplicated cystitis; urine culture in men, children, pregnancy, recurrent or complicated infection; blood tests and imaging if kidney infection or obstruction is suspected. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with a urinalysis and, where indicated, a urine culture, which usually takes several days to complete.
urinary-tract-infection.treatment: A short course of antibiotics (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim for cystitis; longer courses of a broader agent for kidney infection), fluids and pain relief. Intravenous antibiotics for severe infection; relief of any obstruction. Cystitis often gets better by itself, and UK services may issue a delayed ('back-up') antibiotic prescription to be started only if symptoms do not settle. Paracetamol eases the discomfort. Complicated infection may need a longer course or intravenous antibiotics, and persistent symptoms warrant further testing rather than repeated empirical courses.
urinary-tract-infection.prevention: Fluids, emptying the bladder after sex, avoiding spermicides, vaginal oestrogen after the menopause, prophylactic antibiotics or methenamine for frequent recurrences. NHS advice also includes avoiding perfumed bubble bath, soap or talcum powder around the genitals, preferring showers to baths, passing urine as soon as the urge is felt and wiping from front to back; for some women with recurrent cystitis a single antibiotic dose taken after sex is prescribed.
urinary-tract-infection.seekCare: Urgent care for fever, shivering, loin pain, vomiting or confusion with urinary symptoms, symptoms in pregnancy or in a man, or blood in the urine that persists.

sections.heading: What does a UTI feel like?
sections.body:
NHS guidance lists pain or a burning feeling when passing urine, needing to go more often than usual, cloudy urine, blood in the urine, and pain in the lower tummy or in the back just under the ribs. Feeling tired or weak and smelly urine can also occur. NIDDK, a US health institute, describes similar bladder infection symptoms, including discomfort in the lower abdomen and cloudy, bloody or strong-smelling urine.

When a bladder infection spreads to one or both kidneys, NIDDK lists fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin as warning signs. It says early treatment prevents most complications. MedlinePlus says bladder infection symptoms usually improve within a day or two of starting treatment, while kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve.

sections.heading: How does a UTI show up in older people and children?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says older adults may show only confusion. The NHS says that in older, frail people with memory problems such as dementia, and in people with a urinary catheter, symptoms can include changes in behaviour such as acting agitated or confused, wetting that is worse than usual, or new shivering or shaking.

In babies and young children, fever is the most common sign and may be the only one. Poor feeding and vomiting can also occur. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says antibiotics for a child's UTI should start quickly to protect the kidneys, and a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

sections.heading: How is a UTI diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes urinary tract infections as affecting the bladder, kidneys, ureters or urethra, and calls a kidney infection pyelonephritis. A urine culture identifies the bacteria so a clinician can choose an antibiotic. A positive culture, meaning bacteria or yeast grew, likely indicates a UTI, although earlier antibiotic use can produce a falsely negative result.

For older adults, the NICE quality standard recommends diagnosing UTI by full clinical assessment, without a urine dipstick test, because dipstick accuracy varies. A UK hospital study of older patients found that most positive dipstick results did not match the laboratory result. The NHS England and UKHSA toolkit likewise says dipsticks should be avoided in older adults to support an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
NIDDK says a health professional will likely prescribe antibiotics for a bacterial bladder infection, and the length of treatment depends on how severe the infection is and whether symptoms go away. It advises finishing the whole course, because antibiotic resistance could make an infection harder to treat, and says drinking more liquids, with water best, can speed recovery and ease symptoms.

The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone.

For kidney infection, the NHS says most people are treated at home with antibiotics. Paracetamol helps with pain and high temperature, and ibuprofen-type painkillers are not normally recommended because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems. Hospital treatment with antibiotics through a drip may be needed for people who are pregnant, have a long-term health condition, are severely dehydrated or cannot keep down fluids or medicines.

sections.heading: Why do some people get UTIs again and again?
sections.body:
Reviews define recurrent UTI as two infections within six months or three within twelve months. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if a UTI returns after treatment or follows that pattern. Options it lists include a different antibiotic, a low-dose antibiotic taken for up to six months, or, after the menopause, an oestrogen vaginal product. NHS patient information also describes taking antibiotics after sex where sex seems to trigger infections.

NIDDK says vaginal oestrogen increases good bacteria and helps prevent infection, and that diaphragms, unlubricated condoms or spermicide may raise the chance of a bladder infection. It says cranberry products do not treat an existing infection and there is not enough evidence to be sure they prevent one.

sections.heading: Can a UTI become serious, and who should be contacted?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus lists kidney infection and sepsis, a dangerous overreaction to infection, as risks of a UTI, with sepsis risk greatest in young children, very old adults and people with weakened immunity. NHS England says older adults made up almost three fifths of UTI hospital admissions over five years.

NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E if a person with a suspected UTI, or their child, is confused, drowsy or has difficulty speaking, and not driving themselves. NHS guidance advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, vomiting, blood in the urine, passing no urine all day, or symptoms that get worse quickly or do not improve within 48 hours. NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days.

faqs.q: Can a UTI get better without antibiotics?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says antibiotics may treat UTIs but are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone. NHS guidance says symptoms that do not improve within 48 hours need review by a GP or NHS 111.

faqs.q: How is a kidney infection different from a bladder infection?
faqs.a: NIDDK says a bladder infection can spread to one or both kidneys, with warning signs of fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin. MedlinePlus says kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve. The NHS describes blood poisoning as a medical emergency.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a UTI in babies and children?
faqs.a: Fever is the most common sign in children under one and may be the only one, with poor feeding and vomiting also possible. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

faqs.q: When should someone see a GP about a UTI?
faqs.a: NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days, or if there is a high temperature, symptoms suddenly worsen, or the person is pregnant or has diabetes. NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E for confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking.

kidney-stones.name: Kidney stones
kidney-stones.definition: Hard crystals, most commonly calcium oxalate, that form in the kidney and can pass into and block the ureter.
kidney-stones.overview: Stones form when urine is concentrated and rich in stone-forming salts. A stone leaving the kidney scrapes and blocks the ureter, producing renal colic: waves of agonising pain from the loin to the groin with blood in the urine. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own; larger or infected obstructions need intervention. Stones form when urine carries high concentrations of calcium, oxalate or phosphate, although in many individuals no specific reason is ever found. Many small stones cause no symptoms and are passed unnoticed. Pain that comes in waves and radiates from the back or side towards the groin usually means a stone has moved into the ureter; blood in the urine, nausea and vomiting and pain on passing urine are common, and fever or chills point to infection alongside the stone, which changes the urgency entirely.
causes: Low urine volume
High urinary calcium, oxalate or uric acid
Urinary infection with urease-producing bacteria (struvite stones)
Rare inherited causes (cystinuria)
Metabolic conditions such as hyperparathyroidism that raise urinary calcium
riskFactors: High salt, animal protein and oxalate intake
Vigorous exercise or a hot environment without replacing fluid
A first stone at a young age
signs: Restless, unable to lie still
Loin tenderness
Blood in the urine on dipstick
Fever if infected
complications: Obstruction with infection (an emergency)
Kidney damage
Recurrence in half within ten years
Acute kidney injury with reduced urine output when drainage is blocked
kidney-stones.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract is the definitive test; ultrasound in pregnancy and children; urine dipstick and culture, kidney function and calcium and urate levels; analysis of the passed stone. Assessment begins with the history, including existing conditions, current medicines, diet and whether relatives have had stones, and with examination. Blood tests check calcium, phosphate, uric acid and electrolytes; urinalysis looks for crystals and red blood cells. Non-contrast CT is the preferred imaging test to confirm a stone and check for obstruction; ultrasound is used first in children and in pregnancy to avoid radiation.
kidney-stones.treatment: Strong analgesia (NSAIDs are most effective), fluids, and drugs to relax the ureter to help small stones pass; shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation or percutaneous surgery for larger stones; urgent drainage with a stent or nephrostomy if obstructed and infected. Stone size is the main determinant of initial treatment, and most small stones pass spontaneously. Alpha blockers and calcium-channel blockers can aid passage by relaxing the ureter. Stones unlikely to pass are candidates for minimally invasive treatment such as shock-wave lithotripsy. For adults with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium, NICE CKS advises considering a thiazide once salt intake has been reduced; potassium citrate and allopurinol are used for other recurrent stone types.
kidney-stones.prevention: Drink enough to pass 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day, limit salt and animal protein, keep normal calcium intake, lemon juice for citrate; specific drugs for recurrent formers. Recurrence is common, approaching half of people within ten years, which is why fluid intake, dietary review and, for repeated stones, metabolic assessment with targeted medication are emphasised.
kidney-stones.seekCare: Emergency care for colicky pain with fever or shivering, vomiting preventing fluids, pain not controlled by painkillers, or a single functioning kidney. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for severe pain or for fever and chills. Unrelieved pain, reduced urine output, infection or acute kidney failure in the presence of an obstructing stone are medical emergencies.

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease
chronic-kidney-disease.definition: Persistent reduction in kidney function (a filtration rate below 60 ml/min) or evidence of kidney damage such as protein in the urine, for more than three months.
chronic-kidney-disease.overview: The kidneys lose nephrons slowly and silently, most often from diabetes and high blood pressure. Symptoms appear only when function is severely reduced, so CKD is found by blood and urine tests in at-risk people. Progression can be slowed for years; a minority reach kidney failure needing dialysis or transplantation. Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys are damaged or structurally abnormal and cannot filter blood as they should, with function declining over months to years. Because early disease causes no symptoms, NHS guidance recommends testing for people with high blood pressure, diabetes or a family history of kidney disease. When symptoms do appear in advanced disease they are non-specific: tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands from fluid retention, shortness of breath, nausea, loss of appetite and blood in the urine, all of which overlap with many less serious conditions. An episode of acute kidney injury can also leave lasting damage that becomes CKD.

High blood pressure
Glomerulonephritis
Polycystic kidney disease
Obstruction (prostate, stones)
Recurrent infection, drugs (NSAIDs, lithium), reflux
Acute kidney injury that does not fully recover
riskFactors: Black, South Asian and Indigenous ancestry
signs: High blood pressure
Oedema
Pallor from anaemia
Late: itching, muscle twitching, drowsiness
Blood in the urine
complications: Cardiovascular disease (the leading cause of death in CKD)
Anaemia
Bone disease and fractures
High potassium, acidosis, fluid overload
End-stage kidney failure
Stroke
Increased susceptibility to infection
Low calcium and high phosphate levels
Loss of appetite and depression
chronic-kidney-disease.diagnosis: Estimated GFR from blood creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, repeated over three months; the two together both make the diagnosis and set its severity, staged G1 to G5 by filtration rate and A1 to A3 by albuminuria. Albumin is a protein that passes into the urine when the filtering units are damaged, so it is an early marker even while the eGFR is still normal. Testing is the only reliable way to know how well the kidneys are working, which is why at-risk groups are screened rather than waiting for symptoms. Ultrasound of the kidneys shows size, obstruction and cysts, and further tests look for the cause, because the cause changes management.
chronic-kidney-disease.treatment: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, statins, glucose control, salt restriction, stopping smoking, avoiding NSAIDs, dose adjustment of medicines; treating anaemia and bone disease; preparing for dialysis or transplantation as function declines. CKD cannot be cured, but progression can often be slowed for years. NIDDK describes blood pressure control as the most important single step; ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the usual choice because they also reduce protein leak, and loop diuretics manage fluid. Blood glucose and cholesterol are treated alongside. Lifestyle measures include lower-salt food, limiting alcohol, staying physically active and not smoking. Anaemia, bone and mineral disorder and fluid overload are treated as they arise. When function falls far enough (kidney failure), dialysis or a kidney transplant is needed for survival, and preparation begins well in advance.
chronic-kidney-disease.prevention: Control diabetes and blood pressure, keep a healthy weight, do not smoke, avoid regular NSAIDs, stay hydrated during illness, have kidney checks if at risk. People with diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of kidney disease are offered regular eGFR and urine albumin checks so that damage is found early.
chronic-kidney-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness, or a sudden fall in urine output; routine review for swelling, frothy urine or persistently high blood pressure. CKD is usually found by routine testing rather than symptoms, so people in at-risk groups are advised to ask about kidney checks.
